name: Physics
tagline: Why things move, shine, fall and hold together.

nodes.title: Pushes and Pulls
nodes.goal: Feel how forces start and stop motion.
nodes.kid_text: When you push a toy car, it zooms away, and when you grab it, it stops. A push sends things away from you and a pull brings them closer. Nothing moves or stops all by itself. It needs your push or your pull to get going!

quiz.prompt: You push the toy car 🚗. It goes…
choices: Away
Closer
Nowhere
quiz.answer: Away
quiz.say: You give the little toy car a push. Does it go away from you, come closer to you, or nowhere at all?
quiz.explain: Yes! A push always sends things away from you.

quiz.prompt: Tug the rope 🪢. That is a…
choices: Pull
Push
Drop
quiz.answer: Pull
quiz.say: In tug of war you grab the rope and bring it toward you. Is that a pull, a push, or a drop?
quiz.explain: That's a pull — a pull brings things closer to you.

quiz.prompt: A still ball 🏀 starts rolling. Why?
choices: A push
It moved by itself
It got heavier
quiz.answer: A push
quiz.say: A ball is sitting still on the floor, and now it starts rolling. Was it a push, did it move by itself, or did it get heavier?
quiz.explain: Nothing moves by itself — it needs a push or a pull.

quiz.prompt: Pull the wagon 🛒 rope. The wagon comes…
choices: Closer
Away
Nowhere
quiz.answer: Closer
quiz.say: You grab the wagon's rope and pull it. Does the wagon come closer to you, go away from you, or nowhere at all?
quiz.explain: A pull always brings things closer to you.

quiz.prompt: You squash the play dough flat. That is a…
choices: Push
Pull
Neither
quiz.answer: Push
quiz.say: You press down hard on the play dough to squash it flat. Is that a push, a pull, or neither one?
quiz.explain: Pressing down is a push — pushes can squash things too.

quiz.prompt: You catch the rolling ball ⚽. It…
choices: Stops
Rolls faster
Rolls the same
quiz.answer: Stops
quiz.say: A ball rolls toward you and you grab it with your hands. Which happens: it stops, it rolls faster, or it rolls the same?
quiz.explain: Your hands pull on the ball, so it stops.

quiz.prompt: Open the fridge door toward you. That is a…
choices: Pull
Push
Lift
quiz.answer: Pull
quiz.say: You open the fridge door by bringing it toward you. Is that a pull, a push, or a lift?
quiz.explain: Bringing something toward you is always a pull.

lesson_media.alt: Three force diagrams compare balanced pushes, an unbalanced push, and compression from opposing pushes.
lesson_media.caption: Arrow length exposes the net force: equal pushes cancel, while unequal pushes change motion and inward pushes squeeze.

lesson_media.title: Force Balance Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change the rightward push, compare it with the fixed 4 N leftward push, and watch the net force change.

nodes.title: Light and Shadow
nodes.goal: Play with light: where do shadows come from?
nodes.kid_text: A shadow is the dark shape that hides behind you when you stand in the sunshine. Light zooms in straight lines, and when your body blocks it, the light can't get through. So a dark you-shaped spot appears on the ground! Move closer to the light and watch your shadow grow big and tall.

lesson_media.alt: A lantern shines past a wooden rabbit cutout and casts a larger rabbit-shaped shadow on a screen behind it.
lesson_media.caption: The blocker sits between the light and the screen, so the place light cannot reach becomes a shadow.

lesson_media.title: Move the shadow maker
lesson_media.instructions: Move the opaque blocker between a small lamp and a screen. Switch the lamp off and on to test what a shadow needs.

quiz.prompt: What makes a shadow? ☀️🧍
choices: Blocking light
Wind
Water
quiz.answer: Blocking light
quiz.say: A dark you-shaped spot appears on the ground. What makes a shadow? Is it blocking light, is it wind, or is it water?
quiz.explain: Right! Your body blocks the light, so a dark shadow appears.

quiz.prompt: A room with no light at all. You make…
choices: No shadow
A big shadow
A small shadow
quiz.answer: No shadow
quiz.say: Imagine a room that is completely dark, with no light at all. Do you make no shadow, a big shadow, or a small shadow?
quiz.explain: No light means no shadow — you need light first!

quiz.prompt: Step close to the lamp 💡. Your shadow gets…
choices: Bigger
Smaller
Brighter
quiz.answer: Bigger
quiz.say: You walk right up close to a bright lamp. Does your shadow get bigger, get smaller, or get brighter?
quiz.explain: Close to the light, your shadow grows big and tall!

quiz.prompt: Torch shines on your hand 🤚. The shadow lands…
choices: Behind your hand
On your hand
On the torch
quiz.answer: Behind your hand
quiz.say: You hold your hand in front of a bright torch. Does the shadow land behind your hand, on your hand, or on the torch?
quiz.explain: Light is blocked by your hand, so the dark shape falls behind it.

quiz.prompt: Step far from the lamp 💡. Your shadow gets…
choices: Smaller
Bigger
Brighter
quiz.answer: Smaller
quiz.say: You walk far, far away from the lamp. Does your shadow get smaller, get bigger, or get brighter?
quiz.explain: Far from the light, your shadow shrinks down small.

quiz.prompt: Light travels in lines that are…
choices: Straight
Wiggly
Curly
quiz.answer: Straight
quiz.say: Light zooms from the lamp all the way to the floor. Does it go in straight lines, wiggly lines, or curly lines?
quiz.explain: Light always zooms along in straight lines.

quiz.prompt: Clouds ☁️ hide the sun. Your shadow…
choices: Fades
Gets darker
Gets bigger
quiz.answer: Fades
quiz.say: Big clouds cover up the sun. Your shadow fades, gets darker, or gets bigger — which one?
quiz.explain: Less light means your shadow fades — no light, no shadow.

nodes.title: Hot and Cold
nodes.goal: Notice heat moving from warm things to cool things.
nodes.kid_text: When you hold a warm cup of cocoa, your cold hands slowly get warm. That is heat sneaking from the hot cup into your fingers. Heat always moves from warmer things to cooler things until they feel the same. That is also why an ice cube melts in your warm hand!

quiz.prompt: Which is hot? 🔥 🧊 🍦
quiz.say: Look at these three things. Which one is hot? The fire 🔥, the ice cube 🧊, or the ice cream 🍦?
quiz.explain: Fire is hot. Ice cubes and ice cream are both cold.

quiz.prompt: Cold hands hold warm cocoa ☕. Hands feel…
choices: Warmer
Colder
The same
quiz.answer: Warmer
quiz.say: Your hands are chilly, and you wrap them around a warm cup of cocoa. Do your hands feel warmer, colder, or the same?
quiz.explain: Heat sneaks from the warm cup into your cool hands.

quiz.prompt: Ice cube 🧊 in your warm hand. It…
choices: Melts
Freezes harder
Stays the same
quiz.answer: Melts
quiz.say: You hold an ice cube in your warm hand. Which happens: it melts, it freezes harder, or it stays the same?
quiz.explain: Your warm hand gives heat to the ice, so it melts.

quiz.prompt: Which one is cold? ☀️ ❄️ 🕯️
quiz.say: Look at these three things. Which one is cold? The snowflake ❄️, the sun ☀️, or the candle 🕯️?
quiz.explain: The snowflake is cold. The sun and the candle are both hot.

quiz.prompt: Hot pizza 🍕 left on the table gets…
choices: Colder
Hotter
Just as hot
quiz.answer: Colder
quiz.say: You leave a hot slice of pizza on the table for a long time. Does it get colder, get hotter, or stay just as hot?
quiz.explain: Heat leaves the warm pizza and sneaks into the cooler room.

quiz.prompt: Heat moves from warm things to…
choices: Cooler things
Warmer things
Nowhere
quiz.answer: Cooler things
quiz.say: Heat loves to travel. Does it move to cooler things, to warmer things, or nowhere at all?
quiz.explain: Heat always travels from warmer things to cooler ones.

quiz.prompt: You blow on hot soup 🍲 to…
choices: Cool it down
Heat it up
Keep it hot
quiz.answer: Cool it down
quiz.say: You blow on your soup before you eat it. Are you trying to cool it down, heat it up, or keep it hot?
quiz.explain: Blowing helps the heat leave, so the soup cools down.

lesson_media.alt: Equal-heat-capacity objects at eighty and twenty degrees approach a shared fifty-degree equilibrium temperature.
lesson_media.caption: For this insulated equal-capacity pair, thermal energy flows hot to cold until equal temperatures remove net transfer.

lesson_media.title: Thermal Contact Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Advance contact time and follow the two temperatures toward thermal equilibrium.

nodes.title: Floating and Sinking
nodes.goal: Guess and test what floats in the bath.
nodes.kid_text: Drop a rubber duck in the bath and it bobs on top, but a stone sinks straight down. The water pushes up on everything, and if a thing is light enough for its size, the water holds it up so it floats. Big puffy things full of air, like a beach ball, float best. Try guessing first, then splash it in to see!

quiz.prompt: Rubber duck 🦆 in the bath. It…
choices: Floats on top
Sinks to the bottom
Stays halfway
quiz.answer: Floats on top
quiz.say: You drop a rubber duck into the bath. It floats on top, sinks to the bottom, or stays halfway — which one?
quiz.explain: The duck is light and full of air, so the water holds it up.

quiz.prompt: Heavy stone 🪨 in the bath. It…
choices: Sinks to the bottom
Floats on top
Stays halfway
quiz.answer: Sinks to the bottom
quiz.say: Now you drop a heavy stone into the bath. It sinks to the bottom, floats on top, or stays halfway — which one?
quiz.explain: The stone is too heavy for its size, so down it goes.

quiz.prompt: Which floats best? 🏐 🔨 🪨
quiz.say: Which one floats best in the water? The big puffy beach ball 🏐, the heavy hammer 🔨, or the stone 🪨?
quiz.explain: Big puffy things full of air, like a beach ball, float the best.

quiz.prompt: Which one floats? 🪵 🔑 🥄
quiz.say: Which one floats on the pond? The wooden stick 🪵, the metal key 🔑, or the metal spoon 🥄?
quiz.explain: Wood is light for its size, so the water holds it up.

quiz.prompt: Drop a metal spoon 🥄 in water. It…
choices: Sinks
Floats
Stays halfway
quiz.answer: Sinks
quiz.say: You drop a heavy metal spoon into a bowl of water. Which happens: it sinks, it floats, or it stays halfway?
quiz.explain: The metal spoon is heavy for its size, so it sinks.

quiz.prompt: Which one sinks? 🍃 🔑 🦆
quiz.say: Which one sinks in the water? The metal key 🔑, the light little leaf 🍃, or the rubber duck 🦆?
quiz.explain: The key is heavy for its size, so down it goes.

quiz.prompt: Water pushes on your bath toys which way?
choices: Up
Down
Sideways
quiz.answer: Up
quiz.say: When you put a toy in the bath, the water pushes on it. Does the water push up, push down, or push sideways?
quiz.explain: Water pushes up on everything — that's what holds floaty things.

lesson_media.alt: Water tanks compare balanced buoyancy and weight, sinking when weight wins, and a clay boat displacing more water.
lesson_media.caption: Floating depends on average density and displaced water, so reshaping the same mass can change whether it floats.

lesson_media.title: Float or Sink Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Reshape a fixed mass by changing displaced volume, then compare weight and buoyancy.

nodes.title: How Things Move
nodes.goal: Speed, direction, and why things stop.
nodes.kid_text: When you run fast, you cover lots of ground quickly, and that is called speed. Moving also has a direction, like running toward the swings, not the slide. Things keep moving until something slows them down, like your feet rubbing the ground or a wall in the way. That rubbing is why a rolling ball always stops in the end.

quiz.prompt: Who moves faster? 🐢 🐇 🐌
quiz.say: Here are three animals. Which one moves fastest? The rabbit 🐇, the turtle 🐢, or the snail 🐌?
quiz.explain: The rabbit is fastest — it covers the most ground in the same time.

quiz.prompt: Two friends race. One gets there first. That one was...
choices: Faster
Slower
Heavier
quiz.answer: Faster
quiz.say: Two friends race to the tree and one gets there first. Was that one faster, slower, or heavier?
quiz.explain: Covering the same distance in less time means moving faster.

quiz.prompt: Why does a rolling ball stop?
choices: Rubbing on the ground
It gets tired
It runs out of push
quiz.answer: Rubbing on the ground
quiz.say: A ball rolls along the floor and slowly stops. Is that because of rubbing on the ground, because it gets tired, or because it runs out of push?
quiz.explain: Rubbing, called friction, slows the ball down — nothing inside it runs out.

quiz.prompt: Which one is slowest? 🐌 🐆 🐇
quiz.say: Here are three animals. Which one is slowest? The snail 🐌, the speedy cheetah 🐆, or the rabbit 🐇?
quiz.explain: The snail is slowest — it covers much less ground in the same time.

quiz.prompt: Running toward the swings 🛝 shows your…
choices: Direction
Speed
Weight
quiz.answer: Direction
quiz.say: You run toward the swings and not toward the slide. Does that show your direction, your speed, or your weight?
quiz.explain: Direction is the way you are heading — toward the swings!

quiz.prompt: A ball rolls furthest on…
choices: Smooth ice
Bumpy grass
Soft sand
quiz.answer: Smooth ice
quiz.say: A ball rolls off at the same speed on three floors. Does it roll furthest on smooth ice, on bumpy grass, or on soft sand?
quiz.explain: Smooth ice rubs the least, so the ball keeps going the longest.

quiz.prompt: You stop pedalling your bike 🚲. You…
choices: Slow down
Speed up
Stay the same
quiz.answer: Slow down
quiz.say: You are riding along and then you stop pedalling. Do you slow down, speed up, or stay the same?
quiz.explain: Rubbing on the road slows you down until you stop.

lesson_media.alt: Equal-time position marks compare the same cart launch across ice, grass, and sand with increasing friction.
lesson_media.caption: More friction transfers kinetic energy faster after an equal launch; shrinking timestamp gaps reveal the greater slowing.

lesson_media.title: Motion and Friction Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change surface friction after the same launch, then compare the position curve.

nodes.title: Simple Machines
nodes.goal: Levers, wheels, ramps and pulleys make work easy.
nodes.kid_text: A simple machine is a clever helper that makes a hard job feel easy. A ramp lets you roll a heavy box up instead of lifting it straight, and a seesaw lever lets you lift a big friend with a little push. Wheels roll so you don't have to drag, and a pulley lets you pull down to lift something up. They don't do magic, they just spread the work out so it feels lighter!

quiz.prompt: Rolling a heavy box up a ramp feels…
choices: Easier than lifting
Harder than lifting
Just the same
quiz.answer: Easier than lifting
quiz.say: You need a heavy box up onto a high step, so you use a ramp. Is that easier than lifting, harder than lifting, or just the same?
quiz.explain: A ramp lets you roll it up slowly instead of lifting it straight.

quiz.prompt: A seesaw is a…
choices: Lever
Ramp
Pulley
quiz.answer: Lever
quiz.say: A seesaw lets you lift a big friend with just a little push. Is a seesaw a lever, a ramp, or a pulley?
quiz.explain: A seesaw is a lever — it spreads the work out so lifting feels easy.

quiz.prompt: Easiest to move across the floor? 🛞 📦 🪨
quiz.say: Which is easiest to move across the floor? Something on round wheels 🛞, a heavy box 📦, or a big stone 🪨?
quiz.explain: Wheels roll along, so you don't have to drag and tug.

quiz.prompt: Pull a pulley rope down. The load goes…
choices: Up
Down
Sideways
quiz.answer: Up
quiz.say: You pull down hard on a pulley rope. Does the heavy load go up, go down, or go sideways?
quiz.explain: A pulley lets you pull down to lift something up.

quiz.prompt: Scissors ✂️ are made of two…
choices: Levers
Ramps
Wheels
quiz.answer: Levers
quiz.say: Scissors have two handles that swing around a middle pin. Are they two levers, two ramps, or two wheels?
quiz.explain: Each scissor handle is a lever, so cutting feels easy.

quiz.prompt: A playground slide 🛝 is really a…
choices: Ramp
Lever
Pulley
quiz.answer: Ramp
quiz.say: A slide is a smooth slope you go down. Is a slide really a ramp, a lever, or a pulley?
quiz.explain: A slide is a ramp — a gentle slope instead of a big drop.

quiz.prompt: Simple machines make hard jobs feel…
choices: Easier
Harder
The same
quiz.answer: Easier
quiz.say: Ramps and wheels and levers all help you. Do they make hard jobs feel easier, harder, or the same?
quiz.explain: They spread the work out, so the job feels lighter.

lesson_media.alt: A ramp, lever, and pulley diagram show smaller force over distance, lever arms, and redirected force.
lesson_media.caption: Simple machines trade force for distance or direction rather than creating work from nothing.

lesson_media.title: Simple Machine Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change the machine geometry to trade force for distance or direction.

nodes.title: Magnets
nodes.goal: Poles, attraction, and compass needles.
nodes.kid_text: A magnet has two ends called poles, a north and a south. If you push two north ends together they shove apart, but a north and a south snap together with a click. Earth is like a giant magnet, so a tiny magnet on a compass always swings to point north. That is how explorers find their way!

quiz.prompt: Two north poles meet. They…
choices: Push apart
Snap together
Do nothing
quiz.answer: Push apart
quiz.say: You push the north end of one magnet against the north end of another magnet. Do they push apart, snap together, or do nothing?
quiz.explain: Two of the same pole always shove each other away.

quiz.prompt: A magnet grabs which one? 🔩 🧸 🪵
quiz.say: Which one will a magnet grab and hold? The metal nail 🔩, the soft teddy bear 🧸, or the wooden log 🪵?
quiz.explain: Magnets pull on iron and steel things like nails, not on toys or wood.

quiz.prompt: Compass needle 🧭 points…
choices: North
South
Straight down
quiz.answer: North
quiz.say: A little magnet on a compass always swings the same way. Does it point north, point south, or point straight down?
quiz.explain: Earth is like a giant magnet, so the needle always finds north.

quiz.prompt: North end meets south end. They…
choices: Snap together
Push apart
Do nothing
quiz.answer: Snap together
quiz.say: You bring the north end of one magnet up to the south end of another. Do they snap together, push apart, or do nothing?
quiz.explain: A north and a south pull together with a click.

quiz.prompt: How many poles does a magnet have?
choices: Two
One
Five
quiz.answer: Two
quiz.say: Every magnet has special ends called poles, a north one and a south one. Is that two poles, one pole, or five poles?
quiz.explain: Two poles — one north and one south.

quiz.prompt: Will a magnet stick to a plastic cup 🥤?
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: No
quiz.say: You hold a magnet against a plastic cup. Does it stick to it? Yes, or no?
quiz.explain: Magnets grab iron and steel things, not plastic ones.

quiz.prompt: Earth acts like one giant…
choices: Magnet
Compass
Iron mountain
quiz.answer: Magnet
quiz.say: Something makes every compass needle swing to the north. Is Earth like a giant magnet, a giant compass, or a giant iron mountain?
quiz.explain: A lump of iron would only tug the needle towards it. A magnet makes it line up north.

lesson_media.alt: Bar magnets show opposite poles attracting, like poles repelling, and curved magnetic field loops.
lesson_media.caption: Pole orientation predicts attraction or repulsion while the surrounding magnetic field always forms closed loops.

lesson_media.title: Magnetic Field Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Rotate the second magnet to inspect how pole orientation changes the interaction.

nodes.title: Sound
nodes.goal: Vibrations you can hear — pitch and loudness.
nodes.kid_text: Every sound starts when something wiggles back and forth really fast, like a guitar string buzzing. That wiggle, called a vibration, shakes the air all the way to your ears. Fast wiggles make a high squeaky sound, and slow wiggles make a low rumbly sound. Pluck a string hard and it wiggles bigger, so the sound gets louder. Speed changes pitch; size changes loudness!

quiz.prompt: Sound starts when something…
choices: Wiggles fast
Sits still
Gets hot
quiz.answer: Wiggles fast
quiz.say: Every single sound begins somehow. Does something wiggle fast, does it sit still, or does it get hot? Say wiggles fast, sits still, or gets hot.
quiz.explain: That fast wiggle is called a vibration, and it makes the sound.

quiz.prompt: Tiny fast wiggles make a sound that is…
choices: High
Low
Quiet
quiz.answer: High
quiz.say: A thin string wiggles in tiny fast wiggles. Does it make a high sound, a low sound, or a quiet sound?
quiz.explain: Fast little wiggles make high squeaky sounds, like a tiny bird.

quiz.prompt: Pluck the string 🎸 harder. The sound gets…
choices: Louder
Higher
Quieter
quiz.answer: Louder
quiz.say: You pluck a guitar string really hard so it wiggles bigger. Does the sound get louder, higher, or quieter?
quiz.explain: Bigger wiggles make a louder sound — plucking harder does not change the note.

quiz.prompt: Slow wiggles make a sound that is…
choices: Low
High
Loud
quiz.answer: Low
quiz.say: A thick string wiggles slowly. Does it make a low sound, a high sound, or a loud sound?
quiz.explain: Slow wiggles make low rumbly sounds.

quiz.prompt: Sound reaches your ears by shaking the…
choices: Air
Light
Nothing
quiz.answer: Air
quiz.say: A wiggle has to travel all the way to your ear. Does it shake the air, shake the light, or shake nothing at all?
quiz.explain: The wiggle shakes the air all the way to your ears.

quiz.prompt: Which makes the highest sound? 🐦 🐘 🦁
quiz.say: Which one makes the highest, squeakiest sound? The little bird 🐦, the big elephant 🐘, or the lion 🦁?
quiz.explain: The little bird's fast wiggles make a high sound.

quiz.prompt: Tap the drum 🥁 gently. The sound is…
choices: Quieter
Louder
Lower
quiz.answer: Quieter
quiz.say: You tap the drum very gently, so the skin only wiggles a little. Is the sound quieter, louder, or lower?
quiz.explain: Small wiggles make a quieter sound.

lesson_media.alt: Air-pressure traces independently compare low and high frequency with small and large amplitude.
lesson_media.caption: The curves graph pressure over time, not sideways air motion: frequency controls pitch and amplitude controls loudness.

lesson_media.title: Sound Wave Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change frequency and amplitude independently to connect pitch and loudness to the wave.

nodes.title: Light and Color
nodes.goal: Rainbows, mirrors and how we see.
nodes.kid_text: Sunlight looks white, but it contains a continuous range of colours. In raindrops, sunlight bends as it enters and leaves and reflects inside; different colours leave at different angles, making a rainbow from red through violet. A smooth mirror reflects light in an orderly direction, and you see its image when that reflected light reaches your eyes. You see most ordinary objects because light from a source reflects from them and enters your eyes.

lesson_media.alt: A lamp sends white light through a slit and glass prism, spreading it downward into red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet toward a screen.
lesson_media.caption: A prism refracts each colour by a different amount; red bends least and violet bends most.

lesson_media.title: Follow the light
lesson_media.instructions: Choose a prism, mirror or toy. Trace where light travels and how it can reach an eye.

quiz.prompt: Sun shines while water drops fall. You see a…
choices: Rainbow
Shadow
Cloud
quiz.answer: Rainbow
quiz.say: The sun is shining and little drops of water are falling from the sky. What do you see up there? A rainbow, a shadow, or a cloud?
quiz.explain: Light refracts as it enters and leaves each drop and reflects inside. Different colours leave at different angles, so together many drops make a rainbow.

quiz.prompt: White sunlight ☀️ is really…
choices: Many colours mixed
One colour only
No colour at all
quiz.answer: Many colours mixed
quiz.say: Sunlight looks plain white. Is it really many colours mixed, one colour only, or no colour at all?
quiz.explain: White sunlight contains a continuous range of colours, from red through violet.

quiz.prompt: You see your own face best in a…
choices: Mirror
Sheet of paper
Woolly jumper
quiz.answer: Mirror
quiz.say: Which one bounces light back so neatly that you see your own face? A mirror, a sheet of paper, or a woolly jumper?
quiz.explain: A smooth mirror reflects light in an orderly direction. When that reflected light reaches your eyes, you see an image.

quiz.prompt: You see a toy because light…
choices: Bounces off it
Stops at it
Comes out of your eyes
quiz.answer: Bounces off it
quiz.say: Light from the lamp lands on your toy. To see it, does light bounce off it, does it stop at it, or does light come out of your eyes? Say bounces off it, stops at it, or comes out of your eyes.
quiz.explain: Light reflects from the toy and some of it enters your eyes. Eyes receive light; they do not send it out.

quiz.prompt: Inside raindrops, sunlight bends and reflects. Then it…
choices: Leaves at different angles as colours
Stops
Turns white
quiz.answer: Leaves at different angles as colours
quiz.say: Sunlight bends and reflects inside a raindrop. Does it leave at different angles as colours, does it stop, or does it turn white?
quiz.explain: Each colour refracts by a different amount, so the colours leave the drop at different angles.

quiz.prompt: Which colour is NOT in a rainbow 🌈?
choices: Brown
Green
Violet
quiz.answer: Brown
quiz.say: One of these is not a rainbow colour at all. Is it brown, green, or violet?
quiz.explain: A rainbow is a continuous spectrum from red through violet. Brown is not a spectral colour.

quiz.prompt: A shiny spoon 🥄 works a bit like a…
choices: Mirror
Window
Torch
quiz.answer: Mirror
quiz.say: You look at a shiny spoon and see your own face. Is it working like a mirror, a window, or a torch?
quiz.explain: A smooth shiny spoon reflects light in an orderly way, a little like a curved mirror; a window mainly lets light through.

nodes.title: Energy Everywhere
nodes.goal: Energy moves and changes form but never vanishes.
nodes.kid_text: Energy is what makes things go, glow, and grow. The food you eat gives your body energy to run and jump, and the sun gives plants energy to grow. Energy never disappears, it just changes its costume, like when a wind-up toy's stored energy turns into zooming motion. So when your toy stops, the energy didn't vanish, it just moved into tiny warmth and sound!

quiz.prompt: What gives your body energy? 🏃
choices: Food
Sleep
Fresh air
quiz.answer: Food
quiz.say: You need energy to run and jump all day. Does that energy come from food, from sleep, or from fresh air?
quiz.explain: The food you eat gives your body its energy to move.

quiz.prompt: Who gives plants 🌱 their energy?
choices: The sun
The moon
The wind
quiz.answer: The sun
quiz.say: Plants need energy to grow big and green. Do they get it from the sun, from the moon, or from the wind?
quiz.explain: The sun's energy helps every plant grow.

quiz.prompt: Wind-up toy stops. Its energy…
choices: Turned into warmth and sound
Vanished forever
Was never there
quiz.answer: Turned into warmth and sound
quiz.say: A wind-up toy runs down and stops. Its energy turned into warmth and sound, vanished forever, or was never there — which one?
quiz.explain: Energy never vanishes — it just changed into a little warmth and sound.

quiz.prompt: Which one stores energy for later? 🔋 🧦 🥄
quiz.say: Which one holds energy inside, ready to use later? The battery 🔋, the sock 🧦, or the spoon 🥄?
quiz.explain: A battery stores energy until you switch something on.

quiz.prompt: Energy can change and move, but it never…
choices: Disappears
Changes
Moves
quiz.answer: Disappears
quiz.say: Energy is busy all day long. Which one does energy never do: disappears, changes, or moves?
quiz.explain: Energy never disappears — it only changes into something else.

quiz.prompt: Rub your hands 🤲 fast. The energy turns into…
choices: Heat
Light
Water
quiz.answer: Heat
quiz.say: You rub your hands together really fast and they start to tingle. Does that energy turn into heat, light, or water?
quiz.explain: Moving energy changes into warmth in your hands.

quiz.prompt: Where does a car 🚗 get its energy?
choices: Fuel
Its wheels
The road
quiz.answer: Fuel
quiz.say: A car needs energy to zoom down the road. Does it come from fuel, from its wheels, or from the road?
quiz.explain: Fuel holds stored energy. The wheels and the road only pass the push along.

lesson_media.alt: Three ten-token bars track gravitational, kinetic, thermal, and surroundings energy before, during, and after movement.
lesson_media.caption: Energy stores change while heating and sound are transfer pathways; a complete account preserves the same total.

lesson_media.title: Energy Transfer Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Move through the transfer and track every unit among gravitational, kinetic, and thermal stores.

nodes.title: Forces and Friction
nodes.goal: Balanced and unbalanced forces; friction and drag.

quiz.prompt: A book sits still on a table. Earth's gravity pulls it down, yet it does not move. What must be true about the forces on the book?
quiz.answer: The table's upward push exactly balances gravity's downward pull.
quiz.explain: Staying still means the forces add to zero, so the upward push equals the downward pull exactly. A larger upward push would accelerate the book upward off the table, and gravity acts on a body whether or not it is falling.
choices: Only gravity acts on the book, but the book is too heavy to move.
The table's push is larger than gravity's pull, which is why it stays put.
There is no gravity acting on the book because it is not falling.
The table's upward push exactly balances gravity's downward pull.

quiz.prompt: You slide a hockey puck across smooth ice and then across a rough carpet with the same starting speed. Why does the puck travel much farther on the ice?
quiz.answer: The ice supplies far less friction to oppose the puck's motion along it.
quiz.explain: A moving object needs no stored push to keep going and carries no force with it. What stops it is friction, a backward force from the surface, and a rough carpet supplies far more of it than smooth ice. Temperature is not what matters; roughness is.
choices: On ice the puck keeps its stored push for longer before it runs out.
Ice is colder, and cold surfaces let things slide more easily.
The carpet soaks up the force the puck was carrying with it.
The ice supplies far less friction to oppose the puck's motion along it.

quiz.prompt: A skydiver falls faster and faster at first, then stops speeding up and drops at a steady speed while gravity still pulls on her. What has happened?
quiz.answer: Air resistance has grown until it balances her weight.
choices: Air resistance now exceeds her weight, so it holds her up.
She has reached the top speed that gravity is able to give.
The energy that was speeding her up has been used up.
Air resistance has grown until it balances her weight.
quiz.explain: Drag grows with speed until it exactly equals weight. The forces then add to zero, so the acceleration is zero and she falls at a steady terminal speed. If drag exceeded weight she would slow down, and gravity has no top speed to give.

quiz.prompt: A heavy crate will not budge when one person pushes it, but begins accelerating when two people push together. What changed?
quiz.answer: The push now beats friction, so the forces are unbalanced.
choices: Friction disappears completely once the crate is moving.
The push now beats friction, so the forces are unbalanced.
Two people supply twice the force, and force is what motion needs.
The first push was too weak to overcome the crate's weight.
quiz.explain: Static friction matches a small push exactly, leaving the crate still. Once the push exceeds the largest friction available, the forces are unbalanced and the crate moves. Friction does not vanish once it slides, and it is friction, not weight, that is opposed.

quiz.prompt: A toy car is pulled forward with a force of 30 N while friction drags it backwards with 12 N. What is the net force on the car, in newtons?
quiz.explain: Forces along the same line subtract when they oppose: 30 N - 12 N = 18 N forward.

quiz.prompt: Rubbing your hands together on a cold day makes them feel warm. Explain what friction is doing.
quiz.answer: Friction resists the sliding of one skin surface over the other, and that turns the energy of movement into heat.
quiz.explain: Friction opposes sliding and converts the kinetic energy of the moving surfaces into thermal energy, so the surfaces warm up.

quiz.prompt: Two children pull on opposite ends of a rope, one with 45 N and the other with 25 N. What is the size of the net force on the rope, in newtons?
quiz.explain: 45 N one way and 25 N the other leave an unbalanced 20 N towards the stronger puller.

quiz.prompt: A cyclist stops pedalling on a flat road and slowly comes to a halt. Which explanation fits?
quiz.answer: Friction in the wheels and air resistance push backwards.
choices: The bicycle uses up the force that was stored inside it.
Gravity pulls the bicycle backwards along the flat road.
Moving things naturally slow down, with no force needed.
Friction in the wheels and air resistance push backwards.
quiz.explain: Something must push backwards for the bike to slow: friction and drag do it. A moving object with no force on it would keep going.

quiz.prompt: Why do running shoes have deep rubber treads on the sole?
quiz.answer: To grip the ground with more friction than a smooth sole.
choices: To cushion the landing so that less force reaches the foot.
To spread the runner's weight over a larger area of ground.
To grip the ground with more friction than a smooth sole.
To cut down the air resistance around the moving foot.
quiz.explain: Treads raise the friction between shoe and ground, which is what lets a runner push backwards without slipping. Cushioning is the job of the midsole, not the tread pattern, and air resistance on a foot is negligible.

quiz.prompt: A parachute opens and the skydiver slows down. Explain, in terms of the forces on her, why she slows.
quiz.answer: The open canopy greatly increases the air resistance pushing up on her. That upward force is now bigger than her weight, so the unbalanced force slows her until the two balance again at a lower steady speed.
quiz.explain: Opening the canopy makes drag exceed weight, so the net force points upward and she decelerates to a new, slower terminal speed.

lesson_media.alt: Free-body diagrams compare a resting book, accelerating crate, and moving skydiver at terminal speed.
lesson_media.caption: Balanced forces preserve velocity even during motion; only a nonzero net force produces acceleration.

lesson_media.title: Net Force Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change applied force and friction to connect the net force to acceleration.

nodes.title: Gravity
nodes.goal: The force that shapes falls, orbits and tides.

quiz.prompt: On the Moon, gravity is about one-sixth as strong as on Earth. An astronaut has a mass of 90 kg. Compared to Earth, on the Moon the astronaut's...
quiz.answer: mass stays 90 kg but weight drops to about one-sixth.
quiz.explain: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location, while weight is the gravitational force on that mass and shrinks where gravity is weaker.
choices: mass becomes about one-sixth but weight stays the same.
both mass and weight stay exactly as they were on Earth.
both mass and weight drop to about one-sixth as much.
mass stays 90 kg but weight drops to about one-sixth.

quiz.prompt: The Moon orbits Earth instead of flying off into space in a straight line. What keeps it in orbit?
quiz.answer: Earth's gravity constantly pulls the Moon into a curved path.
quiz.explain: A speed is not a force and cannot balance one; the pull is unbalanced, which is exactly why the path curves instead of running straight. With no force at all the Moon would fly off in a straight line, and the Moon is not held by magnetism.
choices: The Moon's speed balances Earth's pull, so the two cancel out.
Earth's gravity constantly pulls the Moon into a curved path.
No force acts on the Moon at all, so it naturally circles Earth.
Earth's magnetic field grips the Moon and swings it around.

quiz.prompt: On Earth, gravity gives each kilogram of mass about 10 N of weight. What is the weight, in newtons, of a 6 kg watermelon?
quiz.explain: Weight = mass x gravitational field strength = 6 kg x 10 N/kg = 60 N.

quiz.prompt: The same 6 kg watermelon is carried to the Moon, where each kilogram of mass weighs about 1.6 N. What is its weight there, in newtons?
quiz.explain: 6 kg x 1.6 N/kg = 9.6 N. The mass is unchanged at 6 kg; only the weight falls.

quiz.prompt: Inside a tall glass tube with all the air pumped out, a feather and a hammer are let go at the same instant. What do you see?
quiz.answer: They fall side by side and land at exactly the same moment.
choices: The hammer lands first, since it is heavier.
The feather lands first, since it is lighter.
Both float, because the tube has no air.
They fall side by side and land at exactly the same moment.
quiz.explain: Gravity gives every object the same acceleration. Feathers normally lag because of air resistance, and with the air removed that difference disappears.

quiz.prompt: Along most coasts the sea rises and falls twice each day. What mainly drives this?
quiz.answer: The Moon's gravitational pull on the oceans.
choices: Earth's spin flinging the water outward to the coasts.
Steady winds pushing water across the open sea.
The Moon's gravitational pull on the oceans.
The Sun's pull, which is far stronger than the Moon's.
quiz.explain: The Sun does pull harder overall, but tides depend on the difference in pull across Earth, and the Moon's nearness makes its difference about twice the Sun's. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges, which the spinning planet carries the coast through twice a day.

quiz.prompt: A bag of apples weighs 24 N on Earth, where each kilogram of mass weighs about 10 N. What is the bag's mass, in kilograms?
quiz.explain: Mass = weight divided by 10 N per kilogram, so 24 N corresponds to 2.4 kg.

quiz.prompt: A ball is dropped and falls freely. Gravity adds about 10 metres per second to its speed every second. How fast is it falling, in metres per second, after 3 seconds?
quiz.explain: Three seconds of gaining 10 m/s each second gives 30 m/s.

quiz.prompt: Astronauts on the Space Station float past the windows all day. Why?
quiz.answer: They and the station are falling around Earth together.
choices: There is no gravity at all that far above the ground.
The station spins fast enough to cancel gravity out.
They and the station are falling around Earth together.
They are above the air, and it is air that makes things fall.
quiz.explain: Gravity is still strong up there; the station and everything in it are in continual free fall around Earth, so nothing presses on anything.

quiz.prompt: Jupiter has far more mass than Earth. A rock is weighed on each in turn. The rock...
quiz.answer: weighs more on Jupiter, whose greater mass pulls harder.
choices: weighs more on Jupiter, whose greater mass pulls harder.
weighs the same on both, since mass never changes.
weighs more on Earth, which is closer to the Sun.
weighs more on Earth, which has a solid surface to press on.
quiz.explain: Mass is the same everywhere; weight is the gravitational pull on it, and Jupiter pulls far harder. Weight does not depend on having a surface to rest on, nor on distance from the Sun.

lesson_media.alt: Panels distinguish ten-kilogram mass, different Earth and Moon weights, and sideways free fall around a planet.
lesson_media.caption: Mass is intrinsic, weight depends on gravitational field, and orbit combines inward fall with sideways motion.

lesson_media.title: Mass and Weight Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change mass and gravitational field strength to see weight respond through W = mg.

nodes.title: Electricity
nodes.goal: Circuits, current, and static sparks.

quiz.prompt: In a simple circuit, a battery is connected to a bulb by wires and the bulb lights up. If you cut one wire, why does the bulb go out?
quiz.answer: The circuit is broken, so charge cannot flow in a complete loop.
quiz.explain: Current only flows when there is a complete, unbroken path from one battery terminal to the other; a break stops the flow everywhere.
choices: The circuit is broken, so charge cannot flow in a complete loop.
The bulb uses up the electricity and needs the wire to refill it.
The battery instantly runs out of energy when the wire is cut.
The electricity leaks out of the cut end into the open air.

quiz.prompt: You rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to a wall. This is an example of static electricity because...
quiz.answer: rubbing charges the balloon, which then attracts the neutral wall.
quiz.explain: Rubbing moves electrons onto the balloon. The charged balloon pulls the charges in the wall slightly apart, so the near side becomes oppositely charged and attracts it. Nothing flows continuously, and static charge is not magnetism.
choices: a current flows continuously between the balloon and the wall.
rubbing charges the balloon, which then attracts the neutral wall.
the balloon becomes a magnet and sticks to metal hidden in the wall.
rubbing warms the balloon, and warm rubber grips the wall better.

quiz.prompt: Three 1.5 V cells are joined end to end in a row to make one battery. What is the total voltage, in volts?
quiz.explain: Cells joined in a line add their voltages: 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 4.5 V.

quiz.prompt: A 6 V battery lights two identical bulbs joined one after the other in a single loop. The two bulbs share the voltage equally. How many volts are across one bulb?
quiz.explain: In a single loop the voltages across the parts add up to the battery voltage, so each identical bulb takes 6 V / 2 = 3 V.

quiz.prompt: Two bulbs are wired with one battery in a single loop. When one bulb is unscrewed, both go dark. How are they wired?
quiz.answer: In series: the charge must pass through both bulbs in turn.
choices: In parallel, since they share one battery.
In parallel, since removing one bulb breaks the loop they share.
As a short circuit, which drains the battery.
In series: the charge must pass through both bulbs in turn.
quiz.explain: A series loop offers one path, so breaking it anywhere stops the current everywhere. Parallel branches are separate paths: removing one bulb would leave the other lit, which is exactly what did not happen here.

quiz.prompt: Household wires have a copper core inside a plastic sleeve. Why those two materials?
quiz.answer: Copper conducts the current; plastic insulates the hand.
choices: Copper is magnetic while plastic has no magnetism.
Copper conducts the current; plastic insulates the hand.
Copper stores the charge and plastic lets it out slowly.
Plastic stops the copper from getting hot and melting.
quiz.explain: Copper holds its outer electrons loosely, so charge flows through it easily. Plastic holds its electrons tightly and blocks the current, keeping it in the wire and off your hand. Copper is not magnetic, and neither material stores the charge.

quiz.prompt: Two 1.5 V cells and one 3 V cell are joined end to end in a single row. What is the total voltage, in volts?
quiz.explain: Cells in series add: 1.5 + 1.5 + 3 = 6 V.

quiz.prompt: A battery lights two identical bulbs on separate parallel loops. Each bulb draws 0.4 A. What total current, in amperes, leaves the battery?
quiz.explain: In parallel the branch currents add, so the battery supplies 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8 A.

quiz.prompt: A string of fairy lights keeps glowing when one bulb fails. How must the bulbs be wired?
quiz.answer: In parallel, so each bulb sits on its own loop to the battery.
choices: In parallel, so each bulb sits on its own loop to the battery.
In series, so the charge passes through every bulb in turn.
In series, but with wire thick enough to bridge the dead bulb.
In a single loop with the battery pushing across the gap.
quiz.explain: Parallel branches are independent, so breaking one still leaves complete loops through all the others.

quiz.prompt: You pull off a wool jumper in a dark room and hear tiny crackles and see small sparks. Explain what is happening.
quiz.answer: Rubbing transfers electrons between the wool and your other clothes, leaving them oppositely charged. When the built-up static charge grows large enough it jumps across the small air gap as a spark.
quiz.explain: Friction moves electrons from one surface to the other; the separated static charge then discharges across the gap as a visible, audible spark.

lesson_media.alt: Circuit schematics compare an open path, two bulbs in series, and two parallel current branches.
lesson_media.caption: A closed topology permits current; voltage adds across series elements while current divides among parallel branches.

lesson_media.title: Circuit Relationship Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Open the circuit or change voltage and resistance to see current respond.

nodes.title: Heat and Temperature
nodes.goal: Conduction, convection, radiation.

quiz.prompt: A metal spoon left in a pot of hot soup soon becomes hot at the handle end, even though only the bowl end touches the soup. Which method of heat transfer is this?
quiz.answer: Conduction — heat passes along the solid metal from end to end.
quiz.explain: In a solid, heat travels by conduction as vibrating particles pass energy to their neighbors along the metal.
choices: Evaporation — the heat rides on rising steam up into the handle.
Conduction — heat passes along the solid metal from end to end.
Radiation — the hot soup sends invisible rays along the spoon.
Convection — the hot metal carries heat by flowing like a liquid.

quiz.prompt: A radiator warms a room and you notice the air near the ceiling is warmest. Which explains this best?
quiz.answer: Warm air is less dense, so it rises and carries heat upward.
quiz.explain: Heating makes air expand and become less dense, so it floats up and takes its energy with it: a convection current. Heat has no natural upward direction of its own — in a solid it spreads in every direction equally.
choices: Heat always travels upward, whatever the air happens to do.
Warm air is less dense, so it rises and carries heat upward.
The ceiling is closest to the roof, which traps the heat there.
Warm air is heavier and sinks, pushing cool air to the ceiling.

quiz.prompt: A pot of water starts at 20 degrees Celsius and is heated until the thermometer reads 85 degrees Celsius. By how many degrees Celsius did its temperature rise?
quiz.explain: A temperature change is the difference between the readings: 85 - 20 = 65 degrees Celsius.

quiz.prompt: A metal chair and a wooden chair have stood in the same cool room all night. Why does the metal one feel colder when you sit on it?
quiz.answer: Metal conducts heat away from your skin much faster than wood does, even though both chairs are at the same temperature.
quiz.explain: Both chairs are at room temperature. Metal is the better conductor, so it draws heat out of your skin quickly and your nerves report cold.

quiz.prompt: A vacuum flask has two silvered walls with a vacuum between them, and it keeps soup hot for hours. Which route for heat does the vacuum shut off, and which does the silvering shut off?
quiz.answer: Vacuum blocks conduction and convection; silvering reflects radiation.
choices: Vacuum blocks radiation, while silvering blocks conduction and convection.
Vacuum blocks all three routes; the silvering is only decorative.
Vacuum blocks conduction and convection; silvering reflects radiation.
Silvering blocks all three; the vacuum simply seals the soup in.
quiz.explain: Conduction and convection both need particles, so emptying the gap shuts them off. Radiation crosses a vacuum happily, and it is the mirrored surfaces that turn it back into the soup.

quiz.prompt: The Sun's heat crosses millions of kilometres of empty space to reach Earth. Which method of transfer must be carrying it?
quiz.answer: Radiation, which needs no material to travel through.
choices: Convection, carried by rising currents of warm air.
Conduction, passed on by particles touching each other.
Radiation, which needs no material to travel through.
Evaporation, lifting heat away as water vapour.
quiz.explain: Conduction and convection both need matter to carry the energy. Only radiation, in the form of electromagnetic waves, crosses a vacuum.

quiz.prompt: A cup of tea cools from 90 degrees Celsius to 34 degrees Celsius. By how many degrees Celsius has it fallen?
quiz.explain: 90 - 34 = 56 degrees Celsius.

quiz.prompt: A freezer is at 18 degrees Celsius below zero and a warm room is at 22 degrees Celsius. What is the temperature difference between them, in degrees Celsius?
quiz.explain: From -18 up to 0 is 18 degrees, and 0 up to 22 is 22 more, giving 40 degrees in total.

quiz.prompt: In many hot countries houses are painted white. What does the white paint do?
quiz.answer: It reflects sunlight instead of absorbing it.
choices: It lets more heat pass through the wall to the inside.
It stops the warm air inside from rising up and out.
It reflects sunlight instead of absorbing it.
It conducts heat better, so the warmth spreads out evenly.
quiz.explain: Pale, shiny surfaces reflect radiation; dark surfaces absorb it and get hot.

quiz.prompt: A woolly hat keeps your head warm on a cold day. What is the best explanation?
quiz.answer: Air trapped in the wool conducts heat poorly, slowing the loss.
choices: Air trapped in the wool conducts heat poorly, slowing the loss.
The wool makes heat of its own and passes it to your head.
The wool draws the cold out of the air around your head and holds it.
The wool is warm to start with and shares that warmth.
quiz.explain: Wool works by holding still air, which is a poor conductor, so heat leaves your head more slowly. Nothing makes new heat, and cold is not a substance that can be drawn out — it is simply the absence of heat.

lesson_media.alt: A solid bar, circulating fluid, and radiant rays distinguish conduction, convection, and radiation.
lesson_media.caption: Conduction uses neighboring interactions and mobile electrons in conductors; convection moves fluid, while radiation uses electromagnetic waves.

lesson_media.title: Heat Transfer Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Select a transfer mechanism and vary the temperature gap without treating unlike rates as one ranking.

nodes.title: Waves
nodes.goal: Wavelength, frequency, amplitude — in water, sound and light.

quiz.prompt: A water wave has a wavelength of 2 meters and a frequency of 3 hertz (3 waves pass each second). What is its speed in meters per second? (speed = frequency × wavelength)
quiz.explain: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 3 Hz × 2 m = 6 m/s.

quiz.prompt: Two sound waves travel through the same air. Wave A has a higher frequency than wave B. What will you notice about wave A compared to wave B?
quiz.answer: Wave A has a higher pitch and a shorter wavelength.
quiz.explain: For waves at the same speed, higher frequency means shorter wavelength, and for sound a higher frequency is heard as a higher pitch.
choices: Wave A travels much faster through the same still air.
Wave A is louder but has exactly the same pitch.
Wave A has a lower pitch and a much longer wavelength.
Wave A has a higher pitch and a shorter wavelength.

quiz.prompt: A sound wave travels at 340 metres per second and has a frequency of 170 hertz. What is its wavelength in metres? (wavelength = speed / frequency)
quiz.explain: 340 m/s divided by 170 Hz gives 2 m: each wave stretches 2 metres from crest to crest.

quiz.prompt: In a thunderstorm you see the flash well before you hear the bang, even though the lightning makes both at the same instant. Why?
quiz.answer: Light travels enormously faster than sound, so the flash arrives almost at once while the sound needs time to cover the distance.
quiz.explain: Light covers a kilometre in about three millionths of a second; sound needs about three seconds. The gap you hear is the sound still on its way.

quiz.prompt: You drop a pebble into a still pond. A duck floating a metre away bobs up and down but does not get carried outward. What does this show?
quiz.answer: Energy travels outward while the water only moves up and down.
choices: The wave is not yet strong enough to drag the duck along with it.
Energy travels outward while the water only moves up and down.
The duck floats, and floating things are not pushed by waves.
The water does move outward, but it flows back again just as fast.
quiz.explain: In a wave the energy travels but the medium does not. Each patch of water bobs about its own place and hands the disturbance on to the next, which is why the duck rises and falls without going anywhere.

quiz.prompt: Two notes played on the same instrument sound at the same pitch, but one is much louder. What differs between the two waves?
quiz.answer: Their amplitude, the height of the wave carrying the sound.
choices: Their frequency, counted in hertz each second.
Their wavelength, measured from crest to crest.
Their speed as they cross the still air of the room.
Their amplitude, the height of the wave carrying the sound.
quiz.explain: Loudness is set by amplitude, the height of the wave. Pitch is set by frequency, and since the pitch matched, the frequency and wavelength are the same.

quiz.prompt: A wave machine sends out 12 complete waves in 4 seconds. What is the frequency, in hertz?
quiz.explain: Frequency is waves per second: 12 divided by 4 is 3 Hz.

quiz.prompt: A wave travels at 20 metres per second with a wavelength of 5 metres. What is its frequency, in hertz?
quiz.explain: Frequency = speed divided by wavelength = 20 / 5 = 4 Hz.

quiz.prompt: You shout across a valley and a moment later hear your own voice come back. What happened to the sound?
quiz.answer: It reflected off the far cliff and travelled back.
choices: It bounced off the air in the middle of the valley.
It reflected off the far cliff and travelled back.
It was soaked up by the cliff and given out again later.
It changed into a new sound with a lower pitch.
quiz.explain: An echo is a reflection: the wave bounces off a hard, distant surface and returns. Air does not reflect sound like that, and a surface that absorbed the sound would give you silence, not a delayed copy.

quiz.prompt: Two astronauts standing close together on the Moon's surface cannot hear each other shout. Why not?
quiz.answer: There is no air on the Moon to carry the sound waves.
choices: There is no air on the Moon to carry the sound waves.
Sound travels too slowly in the Moon's low gravity.
The Moon is too cold for sound waves to travel.
Their sealed helmets block the shout before it can leave.
quiz.explain: Sound is a vibration of a material and needs one to travel through. The Moon has essentially no atmosphere, so even with the helmets off there would be nothing to carry the shout. Gravity and temperature are not what matters.

lesson_media.alt: Wave traces show frequency and wavelength trading at fixed speed while amplitude changes independently.
lesson_media.caption: The relation v equals frequency times wavelength constrains spacing; amplitude controls energy without changing that speed.

lesson_media.title: Wave Relationship Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change frequency and amplitude while the model preserves the wave-speed constraint.

nodes.title: States of Matter
nodes.goal: Solid, liquid, gas — and what changes between them.

quiz.prompt: Solid ice, liquid water, and water vapor are all made of the same molecules. What mainly differs between these three states?
quiz.answer: How the molecules are packed and how freely they move.
quiz.explain: The state of matter depends on how tightly particles are packed and how much they move, not on the identity of the molecules.
choices: The chemical formula that describes each of the substances.
The kind of molecules that each substance is made of.
The total number of molecules present in the whole sample.
How the molecules are packed and how freely they move.

quiz.prompt: A puddle of water slowly disappears on a warm day without boiling. What has happened to the water?
quiz.answer: It evaporated, changing from liquid to gas at the surface.
quiz.explain: The fastest molecules at the surface escape into the air as a gas, well below boiling point. Water vapour is a true gas, not a mist of tiny drops, and matter is never destroyed by warmth.
choices: It evaporated, changing from liquid to gas at the surface.
It condensed into a denser liquid that sank into the ground.
It soaked into the air as tiny drops that stay liquid.
It was destroyed by the heat and no longer exists.

quiz.prompt: A metal block has a mass of 24 grams and a volume of 8 cubic centimetres. What is its density, in grams per cubic centimetre?
quiz.explain: Density = mass / volume = 24 g / 8 cm3 = 3 g per cubic centimetre.

quiz.prompt: Ice cubes sit in a freezer at 18 degrees Celsius below zero. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius. By how many degrees Celsius must they be warmed to reach their melting point?
quiz.explain: Going from -18 degrees Celsius up to 0 degrees Celsius is a rise of 18 degrees.

quiz.prompt: A tied balloon is left in a warm room and swells noticeably, though nobody added any air. Why?
quiz.answer: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder.
choices: The warmth creates extra air inside the balloon.
Each particle swells up, so the gas takes more room.
The rubber softens in the heat and stretches on its own.
The particles move faster and hit the walls harder.
quiz.explain: Warming speeds the particles up. They strike the rubber harder and more often, raising the pressure until the balloon stretches. The particles themselves do not change size and no new gas appears — there are exactly as many as before.

quiz.prompt: Steam from a kettle reaches a cold window and tiny drops of water appear on the glass. What is this change of state called?
quiz.answer: Condensation, as vapour cools and turns back to liquid.
choices: Evaporation, from liquid into gas.
Sublimation, from solid straight to gas.
Melting, from solid into liquid.
Condensation, as vapour cools and turns back to liquid.
quiz.explain: Water vapour touching cold glass loses energy, slows down, and gathers into liquid drops. Gas turning into liquid is condensation.

quiz.prompt: A stone has a mass of 150 grams and a volume of 60 cubic centimetres. What is its density, in grams per cubic centimetre?
quiz.explain: Density = mass / volume = 150 / 60 = 2.5 g per cubic centimetre.

quiz.prompt: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. A liquid metal boils at 357 degrees Celsius. By how many degrees Celsius is the metal's boiling point higher?
quiz.explain: 357 - 100 = 257 degrees Celsius.

quiz.prompt: You can squash a sealed syringe full of air, but the same syringe full of water hardly moves. Why?
quiz.answer: Gas particles have big gaps that can be squeezed shut.
choices: Air particles are softer than water particles.
Water particles stick to the walls of the syringe.
Air is lighter, so less force is needed to move it.
Gas particles have big gaps that can be squeezed shut.
quiz.explain: A gas is mostly empty space, so its particles can be pushed closer together. In a liquid they already touch, leaving nothing to close up. Particles are not soft or springy in themselves; it is the spacing that differs.

quiz.prompt: Wet washing dries on the line on a cold but windy day, even though it never gets warm. Why?
quiz.answer: The wind carries the escaping water vapour away.
choices: The wind carries the escaping water vapour away.
Cold air holds more water, so it draws it from the cloth.
The wind is cold, and cold air dries better than warm air.
Water can only leave the cloth once it is heated to boiling.
quiz.explain: Evaporation happens at every temperature. Moving air sweeps the vapour away before it can return to the cloth, so more keeps escaping. Cold air actually holds less water than warm air, which is why warm windy days dry fastest of all.

lesson_media.alt: Identical particles appear ordered in a solid, mobile in a liquid, and widely separated in a gas.
lesson_media.caption: A phase change rearranges spacing and motion rather than changing the identity of the particles.

lesson_media.title: Particle State Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change temperature and inspect particle arrangements and coexistence at the phase boundaries.

nodes.title: Measuring the World
nodes.goal: SI units, precision, and honest measurement.

quiz.prompt: A student reports the length of a table as '1.5'. Why is this measurement not yet useful to a scientist?
quiz.answer: It has no unit, so 1.5 could mean meters, feet, or inches.
quiz.explain: A number on its own says nothing until you know what it is being compared against; the unit supplies that. An uncertainty and extra digits both help, but neither rescues a measurement that could be meters or inches.
choices: A length must always be reported with an uncertainty attached.
It has no unit, so 1.5 could mean meters, feet, or inches.
1.5 is too few digits to describe a real table properly.
A single measurement is never enough to count as scientific.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the SI base unit used to measure mass?
quiz.answer: kg
quiz.explain: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass; the newton measures force, the liter is volume, and the pound is not an SI unit.
choices: N
kg
L
lb

quiz.prompt: A ribbon is 2.5 metres long. How many centimetres is that?
quiz.explain: There are 100 centimetres in a metre, so 2.5 x 100 = 250 cm.

quiz.prompt: A runner covers 400 metres in 50 seconds. What is her average speed, in metres per second?
quiz.explain: Average speed = distance / time = 400 m / 50 s = 8 m/s.

quiz.prompt: Two students measure the same pencil with the same ruler and get 14.2 cm and 14.3 cm. What is the best thing to do with these numbers?
quiz.answer: Average them to about 14.25 cm and note the small spread.
choices: Keep the first reading, since the second was influenced by it.
Average them to about 14.25 cm and note the small spread.
Take the larger value, since a ruler can only under-read.
Measure once more and keep whichever two readings agree.
quiz.explain: Real readings scatter a little, and the mean of repeats is the best estimate while the spread shows how sure you can be. Discarding data because it disagrees, or keeping only the readings that match, throws away exactly that information.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is written with the SI base unit for measuring how long something takes?
choices: 12 min
12 hr
12 Hz
quiz.explain: The second (s) is the SI base unit of time. Minutes and hours are accepted but are not the base unit, and the hertz counts events per second, not time.

quiz.prompt: A shelf is 1.25 metres long. How many millimetres is that?
quiz.explain: One metre is 1000 mm, so 1.25 m is 1250 mm.

quiz.prompt: A walker covers 3 kilometres in 1500 seconds. What is the average speed, in metres per second?
quiz.explain: 3 km is 3000 m; 3000 divided by 1500 is 2 m/s.

quiz.prompt: A student measures a table five times and records 74.1, 74.2, 74.1, 74.2 and 88.0 cm. What is the best thing to do about the 88.0 cm reading?
quiz.answer: Treat it as a likely mistake, then check it by measuring again.
choices: Treat it as a likely mistake, then check it by measuring again.
Keep it in the average, since data must not be thrown out.
Report it on its own, since it stands out from the rest.
Ignore all five and start the whole experiment afresh.
quiz.explain: One reading far from the rest usually signals a slip in reading or recording; the honest move is to repeat the measurement and see.

quiz.prompt: A recipe asks for 250 millilitres of milk, but the jug is marked only in litres. How much should you pour?
quiz.answer: 0.25 litres
choices: 2.5 litres
25 litres
0.025 litres
0.25 litres
quiz.explain: There are 1000 mL in a litre, so 250 mL is a quarter of a litre, 0.25 L.

lesson_media.alt: A ruler resolution, metre-to-centimetre conversion, and repeated readings with an outlier form a measurement audit.
lesson_media.caption: Units preserve meaning, scale limits precision, and repeated measurements reveal variation and possible outliers.

lesson_media.title: Measurement Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change instrument resolution and repeat count to inspect precision and uncertainty.

nodes.title: Newton's Laws
nodes.goal: F = ma and everything it explains.

quiz.prompt: A net force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg cart on a frictionless surface. Using F = ma, what is the cart's acceleration in meters per second squared?
quiz.explain: Rearranging F = ma gives a = F/m = 12 N ÷ 3 kg = 4 m/s².

quiz.prompt: A book rests on a table. The table pushes up on the book with a normal force. By Newton's third law, what is the reaction to this force?
quiz.answer: The book pushes down on the table with an equal force.
quiz.explain: A third-law pair acts on two different bodies; the reaction to the table pushing up on the book is the book pushing down on the table.
choices: The table pushes up on the book a second time as well.
The book pushes down on the table with an equal force.
The Earth pushes the book upward through the table.
Gravity pulls the book downward with an equal force.

quiz.prompt: A car and a loaded truck experience the same net forward force. Which statement about their motion is correct?
quiz.answer: The lighter car accelerates more, because it has less mass.
quiz.explain: From a = F/m, with equal force the smaller mass gains the larger acceleration.
choices: The lighter car accelerates more, because it has less mass.
The heavier truck accelerates more because it has more mass.
Neither one accelerates unless the forces are different.
Both accelerate equally, because the net force is the same.

quiz.prompt: A 1200 kg car speeds up from rest to 20 m/s in 8.0 s at a steady rate. What constant net force, in newtons, does this require?
A car brakes hard and a loose backpack on the rear seat slides forward. A passenger says a force threw it forward. What is the better account?
quiz.answer: No forward force acts; the backpack keeps its own motion.
choices: Braking creates a forward force on the backpack.
The backpack gains momentum as the car slows down.
Friction from the seat pushes the backpack ahead.
No forward force acts; the backpack keeps its own motion.
quiz.explain: By Newton's first law the backpack carries on at the velocity it already had. The car decelerates underneath it, so the dashboard comes to meet the backpack. Friction from the seat acts backwards on it, not forwards.

quiz.prompt: An astronaut coasting in deep space, far from any star, gives a floating 5 kg toolbox one brief push. Afterwards the toolbox
quiz.answer: drifts on at a steady speed, since nothing acts to slow it.
choices: slows down gradually and eventually stops.
keeps accelerating for as long as it moves.
drifts on at a steady speed, since nothing acts to slow it.
curves back to the astronaut after a while.
quiz.explain: Once the push ends, no net force acts. Newton's first law then requires constant velocity: the toolbox keeps its speed and direction indefinitely.

quiz.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball is struck and accelerates at 60 m/s squared. What net force, in newtons, acts on it?
A 70 kg sprinter accelerates steadily from rest to 9.0 m/s in 3.0 s. What net force, in newtons, is required?
A rocket in deep space fires its engine and speeds up, although there is no air outside to push against. Which statement explains this correctly?
quiz.answer: The rocket pushes the gas backwards, and the gas pushes it forwards.
choices: The rocket pushes the gas backwards, and the gas pushes it forwards.
The exhaust gas pushes against the vacuum outside the nozzle.
The rocket loses mass, and losing mass makes anything speed up.
Momentum builds up inside the rocket and then leaks forward.
quiz.explain: Newton's third law: the engine throws mass one way and takes an equal push the other. No outside medium is needed, which is why rockets work best in vacuum. Shedding mass alone accelerates nothing.

quiz.prompt: A lift accelerates upwards and the passenger feels heavier against the floor. What is actually happening?
quiz.answer: The floor pushes up harder than the passenger's weight.
choices: Gravity grows stronger while the lift is speeding up.
The passenger's mass increases while the lift accelerates.
The push and the weight stay equal, but both of them grow.
The floor pushes up harder than the passenger's weight.
quiz.explain: Upward acceleration needs a net upward force, so the normal force exceeds the weight; the extra push is what feels like extra weight.

lesson_media.alt: Three system diagrams connect constant velocity, force divided by mass, and equal opposite interaction forces.
lesson_media.caption: Zero net force means constant velocity—not necessarily rest; nonzero net force produces acceleration, and interaction forces act on different bodies.

lesson_media.title: Force and Motion Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change force and mass to test Newton's second law and its limiting cases.

nodes.title: Work, Energy and Momentum
nodes.goal: Conservation laws — physics' accounting rules.

quiz.prompt: A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², what is its kinetic energy in joules just before it hits the ground?
quiz.explain: All gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy: mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J.

quiz.prompt: A 4 kg cart moving at 3 m/s collides and sticks to an identical 4 kg cart at rest on a frictionless track. Using conservation of momentum, what is their common speed after the collision?
quiz.explain: Momentum before (4×3 = 12) equals momentum after (8×v), so v = 12/8 = 1.5 m/s.
choices: 3 m/s
6 m/s

quiz.prompt: You push a heavy crate with a force of 50 N, but it does not budge. How much work do you do on the crate?
quiz.answer: Zero, because work requires movement of the crate.
quiz.explain: Work equals force times displacement; with zero displacement, no mechanical work is done regardless of the force applied.
choices: Enough to raise the crate's stored potential energy.
50 J, because you applied a steady force of 50 N.
Zero, because work requires movement of the crate.
It depends only on how long you keep on pushing.

quiz.prompt: A 60 W lamp is left switched on for 5.0 minutes. How many joules of electrical energy does it use?
quiz.explain: Energy = power x time. Five minutes is 300 s, so 60 W x 300 s = 18000 J.

quiz.prompt: A pendulum bob swings down from its highest point to the lowest point of its arc. Compared with the highest point, at the lowest point it has
quiz.answer: less potential energy and more kinetic energy.
choices: more potential energy and less kinetic energy.
more of both kinetic and potential energy.
less of both, since the swing loses energy.
less potential energy and more kinetic energy.
quiz.explain: Falling converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy, so one store empties as the other fills. Air resistance and pivot friction transfer a little mechanical energy into internal energy of the surroundings; the wider total stays unchanged, so the bob very nearly regains its old height.

quiz.prompt: An egg dropped on concrete breaks, but the same egg dropped from the same height onto a thick foam pad survives. The foam helps because it
quiz.answer: stretches out the stopping time, cutting the force.
choices: soaks up the momentum the egg had before landing.
stretches out the stopping time, cutting the force.
reduces the change in momentum that the egg undergoes.
lowers the speed at which the egg reaches the surface.
quiz.explain: The change in momentum is the same on either surface, since the landing speed is the same. Impulse is force x time, so a longer stop means a smaller force.

quiz.prompt: A crane lifts a 250 kg beam 8.0 m at a steady speed. Taking g = 10 m/s squared, how much work, in joules, is done against gravity?
quiz.explain: Work = force x distance = (250 x 10) x 8.0 = 20000 J.

quiz.prompt: A 1500 kg car travels at 20 m/s. What is its kinetic energy, in joules?
quiz.explain: KE = half x m x v squared = 0.5 x 1500 x 400 = 300000 J.

quiz.prompt: A ball bounces a little lower after every bounce. Where has the missing energy gone?
quiz.answer: Into heat and sound, spread out at each bounce.
choices: Into heat and sound, spread out at each bounce.
It was destroyed on contact with the floor.
It was used up by the force of each bounce.
It stays in the floor as unused potential energy.
quiz.explain: Energy is conserved. Squashing the ball and the floor turns some of it into thermal energy and sound at every impact, so less is left to lift the ball. Energy is never destroyed and forces do not use it up.

quiz.prompt: A rifle recoils backwards as the bullet flies forwards. Which quantity is equal in size for the two?
quiz.answer: Their momentum, equal in size and opposite in direction.
choices: Their kinetic energy, since energy is conserved in the shot.
Their speed, because the push is shared out evenly.
Their momentum, equal in size and opposite in direction.
Their acceleration, since one force acts on both of them.
quiz.explain: Momentum is conserved and starts at zero, so the two momenta are equal and opposite; the light bullet carries far more kinetic energy.

lesson_media.alt: A rolling energy bar and two-body collision distinguish energy transfers from momentum accounting.
lesson_media.caption: Total momentum is conserved in isolated collisions, whereas total kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.

lesson_media.title: Collision Ledger Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change collision elasticity and compare momentum conservation with kinetic-energy accounting.

nodes.title: Electricity and Magnetism
nodes.goal: Fields, circuits, induction — toward Maxwell.

quiz.prompt: You push a bar magnet quickly into a coil of wire connected to a meter, and the meter deflects. If you hold the magnet still inside the coil, what does the meter read?
quiz.answer: Zero, because current is induced only while the flux changes.
quiz.explain: Faraday's law says an EMF is induced by a changing magnetic flux; a stationary magnet gives constant flux and no induced current.
choices: A reversed current, because the magnet has come to rest.
Zero, because current is induced only while the flux changes.
A steady large current, because the magnet is inside the coil.
A current that grows as long as the magnet stays inside.

quiz.prompt: Two long parallel wires carry current in the same direction. What happens between them?
quiz.answer: They attract each other.
quiz.explain: Each wire sits in the other's magnetic field, and parallel currents in the same direction produce an attractive magnetic force.
choices: They attract each other.
There is no force between them.
They repel each other.
They twist to become perpendicular.

quiz.prompt: A resistor of 4 ohms has a voltage of 12 volts across it. Using Ohm's law, what current in amperes flows through it?
quiz.explain: Ohm's law gives I = V/R = 12 V ÷ 4 Ω = 3 A.

quiz.prompt: A 12 V supply drives a current of 0.50 A through a small heater. What power, in watts, does the heater dissipate?
A strong magnet dropped down a vertical copper pipe takes several seconds to emerge, while through an identical plastic pipe it falls in a fraction of a second. Why?
quiz.answer: Induced currents in the copper oppose the magnet’s motion.
choices: Copper is magnetic and attracts the falling magnet upward.
Induced currents in the copper oppose the magnet’s motion.
Air in the copper pipe is compressed and slows the fall.
Friction against the copper wall is far greater than against plastic.
quiz.explain: The falling magnet changes the flux through each ring of the copper, inducing eddy currents. By Lenz's law their field opposes the change, braking the magnet. Copper is not magnetic, and the magnet never touches the wall.

quiz.prompt: A 3 ohm and a 6 ohm resistor are connected in parallel across a battery. How does the combined resistance compare with the 3 ohm resistor on its own?
quiz.answer: It is 2 ohms, below either resistor on its own.
choices: It is 9 ohms, the sum of the two resistances.
It is 4.5 ohms, the average of the two values.
It is 2 ohms, below either resistor on its own.
It is 3 ohms, fixed by the smaller of the two.
quiz.explain: 1/R = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 ohms. Adding a parallel branch always gives the current another route, so the total falls below even the smallest branch. Resistances add only in series.

quiz.prompt: A 240 V supply drives a current of 2.0 A through a heater. What is the heater's resistance, in ohms?
A 5 ohm resistor and a 7 ohm resistor are connected in series. What is the total resistance, in ohms?
quiz.explain: Series resistances add: 5 + 7 = 12 ohms.

quiz.prompt: A transformer with more turns on its secondary coil than on its primary is fed with alternating current. What happens at the output?
quiz.answer: The voltage is stepped up and the current stepped down.
choices: The voltage is stepped up and the current stepped down.
Both the output voltage and the output current rise.
The voltage rises, and the power delivered rises with it.
Nothing happens, because a transformer needs direct current.
quiz.explain: An ideal transformer conserves power, so raising voltage lowers current by the same ratio; it needs a changing current, which AC supplies.

quiz.prompt: A bicycle dynamo lights its lamp only while the wheel is turning. Why?
quiz.answer: A voltage appears only while the flux through the coil changes.
choices: A voltage appears only while the flux through the coil changes.
The lamp needs the mechanical push of the wheel to glow.
The dynamo stores charge, which leaks away once it stops.
The magnet loses its magnetism the moment the wheel halts.
quiz.explain: Faraday's law makes the induced voltage depend on the rate at which flux changes, so a stationary magnet and coil produce nothing however strong the magnet. The wheel supplies the change, not a push that travels to the lamp.

lesson_media.alt: A moving magnet and stationary magnet face identical coils, but only changing magnetic flux induces an emf.
lesson_media.caption: Faraday induction depends on flux-change rate, so a strong unchanging flux produces no induced emf in this stationary coil.

lesson_media.title: Induction Coil Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Move, stop, or reverse the magnet to test how changing flux induces voltage.

nodes.title: Waves and Optics
nodes.goal: Interference, diffraction, lenses and images.

quiz.prompt: In a two-slit experiment with light, a bright fringe appears on the screen where waves from the two slits meet. What must be true at that point?
quiz.answer: The two waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively.
quiz.explain: Bright fringes occur where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, so the waves add crest-to-crest.
choices: The two waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively.
Light from only one of the two slits reaches that point.
The two waves arrive out of phase and cancel each other.
The light has changed its color at that point on the screen.

quiz.prompt: An object is placed beyond twice the focal length of a converging lens. The image formed is...
quiz.answer: real, inverted, and smaller than the object.
