quiz.explain: For a converging lens with the object beyond 2f, the image is real, inverted, and diminished, located between f and 2f on the other side.
choices: virtual, upright, and larger than the object.
virtual, inverted, and smaller.
real, upright, and the same size.
real, inverted, and smaller than the object.

quiz.prompt: When you narrow the single slit that light passes through, the central bright band on the screen becomes wider. Why?
quiz.answer: A narrower slit spreads the waves more, so diffraction increases.
quiz.explain: Spreading grows as the slit width approaches the wavelength, so a narrower slit gives a wider central band. The pattern does dim, but that does not widen it, and the wavelength is fixed by the source.
choices: The wavelength of the light gets shorter at a narrow slit.
A narrower slit lets less light through, dimming the whole pattern evenly.
A narrower slit spreads the waves more, so diffraction increases.
The edges of the slit scatter the light out sideways.

quiz.prompt: A converging lens has a focal length of 10 cm and an object stands 30 cm from it. Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, how far from the lens is the image, in centimetres?
quiz.explain: 1/v = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30, so v = 15 cm on the far side of the lens.

quiz.prompt: A straight stick pushed at an angle into a pond looks sharply bent right where it enters the water. What causes this?
quiz.answer: Light changes speed at the water surface, so its path bends there.
choices: Light changes speed at the water surface, so its path bends there.
The water magnifies the lower part of the stick unevenly.
Light is scattered by the water and arrives from a new angle.
The stick really does bend where the water presses on it.
quiz.explain: Refraction: light slows on entering water, and at an angled boundary that change of speed changes its direction. Your eye traces the arriving ray straight back, so the submerged part looks displaced. The stick itself is unchanged.

quiz.prompt: A thin film of oil on a wet road shows swirling bands of colour in sunlight. The colours appear because
quiz.answer: the two reflected waves interfere with one another.
choices: the two reflected waves interfere with one another.
the oil splits sunlight the way a prism does.
the oil glows with its own colour when lit.
the water underneath scatters light into colours.
quiz.explain: Light reflects from the top and bottom faces of the film. The extra path adds or cancels each wavelength depending on the thickness, so different colours dominate in different places.

quiz.prompt: Light travels at 3.0e8 m/s in vacuum and at 2.0e8 m/s inside a certain glass. What is the refractive index of that glass?
A converging lens of focal length 12 cm has an object placed 24 cm from it. Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, how far in centimetres is the image from the lens?
quiz.explain: 1/12 - 1/24 = 1/24, so v = 24 cm: an object at 2f gives an image at 2f.

quiz.prompt: A diver looking upwards sees the whole sky squeezed into a bright circle, while the rest of the surface looks like a mirror. What causes the mirror-like part?
quiz.answer: Total internal reflection past the critical angle.
choices: The water absorbs all light arriving at shallow angles.
The sky really is brighter straight above the diver.
Total internal reflection past the critical angle.
Diffraction bends the outer rays back down into the water.
quiz.explain: Rays meeting the surface beyond the critical angle cannot escape and are reflected back, so the diver sees the lake bed instead of the sky.

quiz.prompt: Two loudspeakers play the same steady note. Walking along a line in front of them you pass through loud and quiet patches. What is happening?
quiz.answer: Path lengths differ, so the waves arrive in and out of step.
choices: One speaker is simply louder than the other in some directions.
The sound reflects off the walls and returns delayed.
Path lengths differ, so the waves arrive in and out of step.
The frequency drifts, so the note beats against itself.
quiz.explain: This is two-source interference. Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths the waves add and it is loud; where it is a half-odd number they cancel. The pattern is fixed in space, which is what tells it apart from beating in time.

lesson_media.alt: Double-slit paths mark bright and dark path differences beside ray convergence through a thin lens.
lesson_media.caption: Interference follows relative path length, while lens geometry predicts the location and orientation of the image.

lesson_media.title: Interference Bench
lesson_media.instructions: Change path difference and wave amplitude to move between constructive and destructive interference.

nodes.title: Thermodynamics
nodes.goal: The laws no engine can cheat.

quiz.prompt: An inventor claims a heat engine that takes in heat from a single reservoir and converts all of it into work, with no other effect. Which law does this violate?
quiz.answer: The second law of thermodynamics.
quiz.explain: The second law forbids converting heat completely into work with no other change; some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir.
choices: Conservation of momentum.
The second law of thermodynamics.
The first law of thermodynamics.
The zeroth law of thermodynamics.

quiz.prompt: A drop of ink spreads through a glass of water and never spontaneously gathers back into a drop. This is best explained by...
quiz.answer: the overwhelming tendency of an isolated system's entropy to rise.
quiz.explain: The spread-out state has far more microscopic arrangements (higher entropy), and the second law makes such irreversible mixing overwhelmingly likely.
choices: the overwhelming tendency of an isolated system's entropy to rise.
the ink using up all of its stored energy while spreading.
gravity slowly pulling the ink droplet apart in the water.
the first law, since energy must always be conserved.

quiz.prompt: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. By the first law of thermodynamics, by how many joules does its internal energy change?
A heat engine absorbs 800 J from a hot reservoir each cycle and dumps 600 J to the cold one. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
quiz.explain: Work out = 800 - 600 = 200 J, so efficiency = 200/800 = 0.25, that is 25 percent.

quiz.prompt: A refrigerator moves heat out of the cold food inside and dumps it into the warmer kitchen. Does this defeat the second law?
quiz.answer: No: a compressor does work to drive it.
choices: Yes, heat flows from cold to hot, which is banned.
No: a compressor does work to drive it.
No, because entropy does not apply to refrigerators.
Yes, but the violation is far too small to notice.
quiz.explain: The second law forbids heat moving from cold to hot with no other effect. A fridge pays for the transfer with work, and the total entropy of fridge plus kitchen still rises.

quiz.prompt: An ideal gas is compressed rapidly inside a well-insulated cylinder, so no heat enters or leaves. What happens to its temperature?
quiz.answer: It rises, because work done on the gas adds internal energy.
choices: It falls, since the gas is squeezed together.
It stays the same, since no heat entered or left the cylinder.
It rises, because work done on the gas adds internal energy.
It falls, because the volume decreased.
quiz.explain: With Q = 0 the first law leaves the change in internal energy equal to the work done on the gas, which is positive under compression, so the temperature climbs. No heat entering is not the same as no energy entering: work is the other route.

quiz.prompt: A gas has 400 J of work done on it while it gives out 150 J of heat. By how many joules does its internal energy change?
quiz.explain: First law: change in internal energy = heat in + work done on the gas = -150 + 400 = +250 J.

quiz.prompt: An ideal heat engine works between reservoirs at 600 K and 300 K. What is its maximum possible efficiency, as a percentage?
quiz.explain: Carnot efficiency = 1 - 300/600 = 0.50, that is 50 percent.

quiz.prompt: A student proposes cooling a kitchen by leaving the fridge door open. What happens over the next hour?
quiz.answer: The kitchen ends up slightly warmer.
choices: The kitchen ends up slightly warmer.
The kitchen cools, since cold air spills out of the fridge.
Nothing at all changes, because the heat exactly cancels.
The kitchen cools until the fridge motor finally gives up.
quiz.explain: The fridge dumps into the room everything it removes, plus the work the compressor does, so the net effect is heating.

quiz.prompt: A sealed, insulated box holds hot water and cold water in two compartments. The divider is removed and the water mixes. What can you say afterwards?
quiz.answer: The total energy is unchanged, but the entropy of the box has risen.
choices: Both the energy and the entropy of the box are unchanged.
The energy has fallen, because heat flowed from hot to cold.
The entropy has fallen, because the mixture is more uniform.
The total energy is unchanged, but the entropy of the box has risen.
quiz.explain: No energy crosses the insulation, so energy is fixed; the irreversible mixing raises entropy, even though the result looks tidier.

lesson_media.alt: A heat-engine budget sends energy from hot to cold while a graph shows the Carnot efficiency ceiling.
lesson_media.caption: Every engine rejects heat; no real engine exceeds the Carnot bound set by its absolute reservoir temperatures.

lesson_media.title: Heat Engine Budget
lesson_media.instructions: Change reservoir temperatures and compare the engine with the Carnot efficiency bound.

nodes.title: Atoms and Nuclei
nodes.goal: Radioactivity, fission, fusion.

quiz.prompt: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 8 days. If you start with 80 grams, how many grams remain after 24 days?
quiz.explain: 24 days is 3 half-lives, so the amount halves three times: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 grams.

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts nuclear fission and nuclear fusion?
quiz.answer: Fission splits a heavy nucleus; fusion joins light nuclei.
quiz.explain: Fission breaks a large nucleus (like uranium) into fragments, while fusion merges small nuclei (like hydrogen) to form a larger one.
choices: Both fission and fusion split heavy nuclei into fragments.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus; fusion joins light nuclei.
Both fission and fusion combine light nuclei into one.
Fission joins light nuclei; fusion splits a heavy nucleus.

quiz.prompt: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, how do its atomic number and mass number change?
quiz.answer: Atomic number decreases by 2 and mass number decreases by 4.
quiz.explain: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), so emitting it lowers the atomic number by 2 and the mass number by 4.
choices: Atomic number stays the same and mass number decreases by 2.
Atomic number decreases by 2 and mass number decreases by 4.
Atomic number increases by 1 and mass number stays the same.
Atomic number decreases by 1 and mass number decreases by 1.

quiz.prompt: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. A wooden beam contains one quarter of the carbon-14 that living wood has. How old is it, in years?
quiz.explain: One quarter remains after two half-lives, so the age is 2 x 5730 = 11460 years.

quiz.prompt: A smoke detector uses americium-241, an alpha emitter, rather than a gamma source. Why is alpha the sensible choice inside a household device?
quiz.answer: Alphas ionise the air strongly but travel only a few centimetres.
choices: Alphas ionise the air strongly but travel only a few centimetres.
Alphas pass easily through the plastic casing to reach the smoke.
Alphas travel furthest in air, so they reach across the chamber.
Alpha decay releases far less energy, making the source safer.
quiz.explain: A heavy, doubly charged alpha ionises the air in the chamber strongly, which is the current that smoke interrupts, and its range of a few centimetres means almost none escapes the casing. Alphas are the least penetrating and the most energetic per event, not the reverse.

quiz.prompt: In beta-minus decay, a neutron inside the nucleus turns into a proton. How do the atomic number and mass number change?
quiz.answer: Atomic number up 1, mass number unchanged.
choices: Atomic number up 1, mass number unchanged.
Atomic number unchanged, mass number falls by 1.
Atomic number down 1, and the mass number up by 1.
Both the atomic number and the mass number rise by 1.
quiz.explain: A neutron becomes a proton, so the proton count rises by one while the total nucleon count stays the same. The element changes; the mass number does not.

quiz.prompt: A source's activity falls from 800 Bq to 100 Bq in 15 hours. What is the half-life, in hours?
quiz.explain: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 is three halvings in 15 hours, so each takes 5 hours.

quiz.prompt: A uranium-238 nucleus has 92 protons. How many neutrons does it hold?
quiz.explain: Mass number minus atomic number: 238 - 92 = 146 neutrons.

quiz.prompt: A hospital wants a tracer that can be detected from outside the body and does not keep irradiating the patient for long. Which choice fits best?
quiz.answer: A gamma emitter with a half-life of a few hours.
choices: An alpha emitter with a half-life of several years.
A gamma emitter with a half-life of a few hours.
A beta emitter with a half-life of thousands of years.
A gamma emitter with a half-life of many decades.
quiz.explain: Gamma rays escape the body to reach a detector, and a short half-life means the activity fades quickly once the scan is over.

quiz.prompt: Fusion powers the Sun but has proved extremely hard to harness on Earth. What is the central difficulty?
quiz.answer: Nuclei repel electrically, so huge temperatures are needed.
choices: There is no hydrogen on Earth light enough to be fused.
Nuclei repel electrically, so huge temperatures are needed.
Fusion releases less energy per kilogram than fission does.
The reaction absorbs energy rather than releasing it.
quiz.explain: The obstacle is the Coulomb barrier between two positive nuclei; stars beat it with immense gravitational compression, and reactors must reach a hundred million kelvin. Fusion releases more energy per kilogram than fission, and deuterium is abundant in seawater.

lesson_media.alt: The nuclear binding-energy curve peaks in the iron-nickel region beside an ensemble halving from thirty-two to four nuclei.
lesson_media.caption: Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei can move products toward the iron-nickel binding peak; half-life predicts ensemble averages, not individual events.

lesson_media.title: Radioactive Ensemble Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Track the expected ensemble fraction while distinguishing it from unpredictable individual decay times.

nodes.title: Special Relativity: a First Look
nodes.goal: Fast clocks run slow; E = mc².

quiz.prompt: A twin travels on a spaceship at very high speed and returns, while the other twin stays on Earth. According to special relativity, what happens?
quiz.answer: The traveling twin has aged less than the twin who stayed on Earth.
quiz.explain: Moving clocks run slow (time dilation), so the traveling twin experiences less elapsed time and returns younger.
choices: The traveling twin has aged less than the twin who stayed on Earth.
The traveling twin has aged more than the twin on Earth.
Time runs faster on the moving ship than it does on Earth.
Both twins have aged by exactly the same amount of time.

quiz.prompt: A student says that E = mc² means a tiny amount of mass corresponds to a huge amount of energy. Why is the energy so large for a small mass?
quiz.answer: Because the mass is multiplied by the speed of light squared.
quiz.explain: c² is about 9×10¹⁶ m²/s², so even a small mass corresponds to a very large rest energy.
choices: Because the mass is multiplied by the speed of light squared.
Because the energy is divided by the speed of light squared.
Because mass and energy are completely unrelated to each other.
Because c is very small, so squaring it makes the energy small.

quiz.prompt: Two observers moving at different constant velocities each measure the speed of the same light beam. What do they find?
quiz.answer: Both measure the same speed of light, whatever their motion.
quiz.explain: The constancy of the speed of light for every inertial observer is a founding postulate of special relativity, and it is what Michelson and Morley found when they looked for an ether. Light speeds do not add to the observer's own.
choices: The observer moving away from it measures a lower speed.
They agree only if both are at rest in the ether.
The observer moving toward the light measures a higher speed.
Both measure the same speed of light, whatever their motion.

quiz.prompt: A spaceship passes Earth at a speed for which the Lorentz factor is 2. The crew measures the outward trip as 3.0 years of their own time. How many years pass on Earth during that trip?
quiz.explain: Earth measures the moving clock as dilated by the factor of 2: 2 x 3.0 = 6.0 years.

quiz.prompt: A pilot in a very fast jet says her wristwatch is ticking perfectly normally, while ground control says her watch is running slow. Can both be right?
quiz.answer: Yes: in her own frame the watch ticks normally, while the ground frame measures the moving clock as dilated.
quiz.explain: Time dilation is a relation between frames, not a fault in a clock. Every observer finds their own clock normal and finds clocks moving relative to them running slow.

quiz.prompt: A muon created high in the atmosphere reaches the ground even though its short lifetime seems to forbid the journey. Working in the muon's own frame, what explains its arrival?
quiz.answer: The distance to the ground is contracted.
choices: Its lifetime is stretched out by time dilation.
It simply travels a little faster than light.
Its half-life grows longer when it speeds up.
The distance to the ground is contracted.
quiz.explain: In the ground frame the muon's clock runs slow; in the muon's own frame the clock is perfectly normal and it is the atmosphere that is contracted. Both accounts predict the same arrival, but the question asks for the muon's own frame.

quiz.prompt: A particle has a proper lifetime of 2.2 microseconds and moves with a Lorentz factor of 4. What lifetime, in microseconds, does the laboratory measure?
quiz.explain: Time dilation multiplies the proper lifetime by gamma: 2.2 x 4 = 8.8 microseconds.

quiz.prompt: A spacecraft is 120 m long at rest. It flies past a station with a Lorentz factor of 3. What length, in metres, does the station measure?
quiz.explain: Length contraction divides the proper length by gamma: 120 / 3 = 40 m.

quiz.prompt: A student says a fast-moving spaceship 'really' shrinks, so the crew must feel squashed inside it. What is the correct account?
quiz.answer: Each frame measures the other as contracted; the crew notice nothing.
choices: Only the ship truly shrinks, but the crew shrink along with it.
The crew do feel the squeeze, which is what limits fast travel.
Lengths change only while the ship accelerates, not while coasting.
Each frame measures the other as contracted; the crew notice nothing.
quiz.explain: Contraction is a relation between frames, not damage done to an object. In its own rest frame the ship has its full proper length and nothing is squeezed, while the crew measure the passing station as contracted instead.

quiz.prompt: Lightning strikes both ends of a moving train at once according to an observer standing on the platform. What does a passenger sitting in the middle of the train conclude?
quiz.answer: The two strikes were not simultaneous.
choices: The two strikes were not simultaneous.
The strikes were simultaneous, exactly as on the platform.
Only the strike at the front of the train really happened.
Both struck at once, but light from one was blocked on the way.
quiz.explain: Simultaneity is frame dependent: the passenger moves towards the light from one end, so that flash is judged to have happened first.

lesson_media.alt: A resting light clock's vertical round trip is compared with successive moving-clock positions and a longer diagonal light path.
lesson_media.caption: In the frame where the clock moves, invariant light speed makes its longer optical path correspond to more coordinate time.

lesson_media.title: Light Clock Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change relative speed to connect invariant light speed with time dilation.

nodes.title: The Quantum Idea
nodes.goal: Photons, energy levels, wave-particle duality.

quiz.prompt: In the photoelectric effect, dim blue light ejects electrons from a metal but very bright red light does not, no matter how intense. This shows that...
quiz.answer: each photon's energy depends on frequency, not on brightness.
quiz.explain: Photon energy E = hf is set by frequency alone, so a red photon lacks the energy to eject an electron however many of them arrive. Energy does not accumulate in the electron while it waits, which is exactly what the classical picture predicted and what the experiment refuted.
choices: each photon's energy depends on frequency, not on brightness.
brighter light always carries more energy in each photon.
enough red light will eventually build up the energy needed.
electrons respond to the total energy delivered, not frequency.

quiz.prompt: An electron passing through a double slit produces an interference pattern over many detections, yet each electron strikes the screen at a single point. This best illustrates...
quiz.answer: wave-particle duality: electrons act as waves and particles.
quiz.explain: The build-up of an interference pattern from individual point hits demonstrates that electrons have both wave and particle characteristics.
choices: that electrons are classical particles bouncing off the slits.
that electrons are ordinary waves with no particle nature.
wave-particle duality: electrons act as waves and particles.
that the slits themselves are emitting their own light.

quiz.prompt: An atom emits light only at specific, discrete wavelengths rather than a continuous spectrum. What does this reveal about the atom?
quiz.answer: Its electrons occupy fixed, quantized energy levels.
quiz.explain: Each line corresponds to one fixed difference between levels, and the photon carries away exactly that gap. A pure sample of a single element still shows many lines, because one atom has many levels to fall between.
choices: The atom is heating up and glowing across all colors.
Its electrons occupy fixed, quantized energy levels.
Its electrons can take on any energy value at all.
The lines come from different elements mixed in the sample.

quiz.prompt: One transition in an atom emits a photon of energy 3.0 eV and another emits 1.5 eV. Since photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, how many times longer is the second photon's wavelength?
quiz.explain: Halving the energy doubles the wavelength, because E = hc/lambda.

quiz.prompt: In a photoelectric experiment the frequency of the light is held fixed above the threshold while the intensity is doubled. What happens to the ejected electrons?
quiz.answer: Twice as many, each with the same top energy.
choices: Each electron leaves with twice the kinetic energy.
The same number leave, but each carries more energy.
None leave at all until the frequency is also raised.
Twice as many, each with the same top energy.
quiz.explain: Intensity sets the number of photons, so twice the light ejects twice the electrons. Maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency alone, so it is unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Single photons are fired one at a time at a double slit, so slowly that only one is ever in flight. Over many hours the accumulated pattern is
quiz.answer: an interference pattern, built up one localised dot at a time.
choices: two bright bands, one behind each slit.
an interference pattern, built up one localised dot at a time.
a single bright spot in the middle.
a smooth even glow across the screen.
quiz.explain: Each photon lands as a point, yet the probability of where it lands follows a wave passing through both slits, so the fringes emerge from many single hits.

quiz.prompt: A metal has a work function of 2.0 eV. A photon of energy 5.0 eV ejects an electron. What is the electron's maximum kinetic energy, in eV?
quiz.explain: Photon energy minus work function: 5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0 eV.

quiz.prompt: An electron drops from a level at -3.4 eV to a level at -13.6 eV. What is the energy, in eV, of the emitted photon?
quiz.explain: The photon carries the difference: 13.6 - 3.4 = 10.2 eV.

quiz.prompt: A very bright red lamp shone on a photocell ejects no electrons at all, yet a faint ultraviolet lamp does. What must a working model of light include?
quiz.answer: Light arrives in quanta whose energy is set by frequency.
choices: Light heats the metal until electrons boil off its surface.
Brighter light spreads its energy over too many electrons.
Red light is reflected by metals while ultraviolet is absorbed.
Light arrives in quanta whose energy is set by frequency.
quiz.explain: Each photon must clear the work function on its own; brightness raises the number of photons, not the energy of any one of them.

quiz.prompt: A cricket ball has a de Broglie wavelength far too small to detect, while an electron's is easily measured. What accounts for the difference?
quiz.answer: The ball's momentum is huge
choices: The ball's momentum is huge
Only charged objects have a wavelength at all.
The ball is many particles whose waves cancel out exactly.
Large objects move too slowly for any wave to form.
quiz.explain: So h over p is vanishingly small. The de Broglie wavelength is h/p, and Planck's constant is so tiny that any everyday momentum puts the wavelength many orders of magnitude below anything measurable. Neutrons are uncharged and diffract perfectly well, so charge is not the issue.

lesson_media.alt: Photoelectric panels separate the frequency threshold from a same-frequency comparison of photon arrival counts.
lesson_media.caption: Frequency sets each photon's energy and the electron maximum; at fixed frequency, intensity changes arrival rate.

lesson_media.title: Photoelectric Bench
lesson_media.instructions: Change frequency and photon arrival rate independently to test threshold energy and emission count.

nodes.title: Fluid Mechanics
nodes.goal: Pressure, flow, and the physics of liquids and gases in motion.

lesson_media.alt: Water flows left to right through a level wide-narrow-wide tube; arrows lengthen in the throat while three pressure taps show equal levels in the wide sections and a lower level in the throat.
lesson_media.caption: For steady incompressible flow, a smaller cross-sectional area requires greater speed. At the same elevation in an idealized flow, Bernoulli's equation pairs that speed increase with lower static pressure.

lesson_media.title: Compare Venturi flow
lesson_media.instructions: Narrow the throat of a horizontal water tube while the volume flow rate stays fixed. Compare speed and ideal pressure change in the wide section and throat.

quiz.prompt: Measurements around a lifting airplane wing show faster airflow over much of the upper surface than below it. Along appropriate streamlines at similar height, use Bernoulli's relation to predict the pressure difference and its contribution to lift.
quiz.answer: Lower pressure above the wing than below it, producing net upward lift
quiz.explain: Where the upper-surface flow is faster under the stated conditions, its static pressure is lower. Integrating the pressure distribution over the wing contributes a net upward force while the wing-air system also deflects air downward. Bernoulli relates local speed and pressure; curvature alone does not make separated parcels reunite at the trailing edge and is not a complete causal explanation of lift.
choices: Lower pressure above the wing than below it, producing net upward lift
Higher pressure above the wing, pushing the plane downward
Equal pressure on both sides, since total energy is conserved
Pressure depends only on altitude, not on airflow speed

quiz.prompt: The continuity equation for an incompressible fluid says the flow rate (cross-sectional area times speed) is constant along a pipe. A hose's nozzle narrows the opening to one-quarter of its original cross-sectional area. Predict the speed of water exiting the nozzle relative to its speed in the wide part of the hose.
quiz.answer: Four times faster
quiz.explain: Continuity requires A1 v1 = A2 v2 for an incompressible fluid, so if the area drops to one-quarter, the speed must rise by a factor of four to keep the product constant — the same volume of water has to pass through a much smaller opening in the same time.
choices: Four times faster
Twice as fast
The same speed, since pressure adjusts instead
One-quarter as fast

quiz.prompt: Archimedes' principle says a submerged or floating object experiences a buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Explain why a steel ship floats even though steel is much denser than water, and what would need to change for it to sink.
quiz.answer: The ship's hull is shaped to displace a large volume of water — much of that volume is air-filled interior space, not solid steel — so the total weight of water displaced by the hull's shape equals the ship's total weight (steel plus cargo plus air) while the ship floats at equilibrium. What matters for floating is the AVERAGE density of the whole ship (mass divided by the volume it displaces), not the density of the steel alone. If enough water leaks in and replaces that air-filled volume, the displaced-water weight can no longer match the ship's weight at any waterline within the hull, and the ship sinks.
quiz.explain: This is the same reason a solid steel block sinks but a steel bowl floats: shape changes the volume of water displaced, not the material's own density.

quiz.prompt: The Reynolds number Re = (density x speed x length)/viscosity helps characterize whether a flow is laminar or turbulent. An engineer doubles a pipe's flow speed while keeping the fluid, pipe diameter, and everything else fixed. Predict the effect on the Reynolds number and the likelihood of transition in that same pipe.
quiz.answer: Reynolds number doubles, making turbulence more likely
quiz.explain: Reynolds number is directly proportional to speed, so doubling the speed doubles Re. For ordinary pipe flow this moves the system toward or farther through its geometry-dependent transition range, often roughly Re 2000-4000; there is no single universal critical Reynolds number for every flow.
choices: Reynolds number doubles, making turbulence more likely
Reynolds number is unaffected by flow speed
Reynolds number halves, making the flow smoother
Reynolds number depends only on pipe material, not speed

quiz.prompt: Viscosity measures a fluid's resistance to shear. Two identical, sufficiently small spheres fall separately through water and honey, with both flows remaining in the low-Reynolds-number Stokes regime. Which sphere approaches terminal speed sooner, and how do the terminal speeds compare?
quiz.answer: The sphere in honey approaches a much lower terminal speed more quickly
quiz.explain: For a sufficiently small sphere in creeping flow, Stokes' law makes terminal speed inversely proportional to viscosity and the velocity relaxation time smaller in the more viscous fluid. That low-Reynolds-number formula is well suited to the honey case; the qualitative prediction that the honey sphere settles more slowly is robust, but Stokes' numerical scaling must not be extrapolated to a water case whose Reynolds number is no longer small.
choices: The sphere in honey approaches a much lower terminal speed more quickly
Both spheres reach the same terminal velocity, just at different times
The sphere in water reaches terminal velocity sooner and at a lower speed
Viscosity does not affect terminal velocity, only the sphere's density does

quiz.prompt: Water (density 1000 kg/m^3) flows through a wide section of a horizontal pipe at 2 m/s, then through a narrow section where its speed rises to 8 m/s. Neglecting losses and using Bernoulli's equation, the pressure drop is (1/2) x density x (v_narrow^2 - v_wide^2). Give the drop in kilopascals (1 kPa = 1000 Pa), rounded to the nearest whole kPa.
quiz.explain: (1/2)(1000)(8^2 - 2^2) = 500 x (64-4) = 500 x 60 = 30,000 Pa = 30 kPa. This pressure drop in the narrow, fast section is exactly the mechanism a venturi flow meter uses to measure flow speed.

quiz.prompt: A no-slip boundary condition states that a viscous fluid's velocity is exactly zero at a solid, stationary surface it flows past — even air right at an airplane wing's surface is (very nearly) motionless relative to the wing. A student argues this contradicts observing wind blowing strongly a few centimeters above a table. Resolve the apparent contradiction.
quiz.answer: No-slip fixes velocity at the surface; speed rises through a boundary layer whose thickness depends on the flow
quiz.explain: No-slip fixes the fluid's relative velocity at the solid surface itself. Velocity then changes continuously through a boundary layer whose thickness depends on geometry, distance downstream, Reynolds number and the surrounding flow. A strong speed a few centimeters above the table therefore does not contradict zero speed at the wall; that point may be within or beyond the boundary layer in a particular setup.
choices: No-slip fixes velocity at the surface; speed rises through a boundary layer whose thickness depends on the flow
No-slip only applies to liquids, not gases like air
The no-slip condition is a simplification that is not actually true
Wind speed a few centimeters up is an illusion caused by measurement error

quiz.prompt: Pascal's principle says a change in pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout it, apart from hydrostatic height differences. A hydraulic lift has pistons at the same height with areas 10 cm^2 and 200 cm^2. A worker applies 50 N to the small piston. Neglecting losses, predict the force at the large piston.
quiz.explain: The applied pressure change is the same at equal height, so F1/A1 = F2/A2 and F2 = 50 x (200/10) = 1000 N. The ideal 20-fold force multiplication is exchanged for the large piston moving one-twentieth as far because displaced volumes match.

quiz.prompt: Explain why a smoke plume rises smoothly for a short distance and then abruptly breaks into swirling, chaotic eddies further up, in terms of the Reynolds number changing along the plume.
quiz.answer: Close to the source, the smoke moves slowly over a small length scale, so its Reynolds number can be low enough for a laminar region where viscosity damps disturbances. Reynolds number compares viscous versus inertial effects; as the plume's speed and width grow, inertial effects become more important and the flow can transition to a turbulent region. The transition range depends on the plume's geometry, buoyancy and disturbances; there is no universal critical Re shared by pipes, plumes and every obstacle.
quiz.explain: A rising plume can display laminar and turbulent regions in one continuous flow, making Reynolds number's comparison of inertial and viscous effects visible. Its transition should not be assigned the critical value used for a different geometry such as a circular pipe.

quiz.prompt: A drinking straw works because sucking air out lowers the pressure inside it below atmospheric pressure, and atmospheric pressure pushing down on the drink's surface then forces liquid up. A student asks whether a straw could lift a drink to any height, given a strong enough suction. Evaluate the claim, using the fact that atmospheric pressure can support at most about 10.3 meters of water before the pressure difference runs out.
quiz.answer: No — there is a hard ceiling around 10.3 m, set by atmospheric pressure itself, no matter how hard you suck
quiz.explain: The absolute best a suction pump (or a mouth) can do is create a perfect vacuum above the liquid; even then, atmospheric pressure alone can only push a column of water up to about 10.3 meters (this is exactly the same physics behind the mercury barometer's roughly 76 cm column, scaled by mercury being about 13.6 times denser than water). No amount of additional suction beyond a perfect vacuum can push the liquid any higher, since there is nothing left to suck — the limit is set by the atmosphere's pushing power, not the straw or the sucker.
choices: No — there is a hard ceiling around 10.3 m, set by atmospheric pressure itself, no matter how hard you suck
Yes, with unlimited suction strength a straw could lift a drink to any height
The limit depends only on straw diameter, not on atmospheric pressure
The limit applies only to mercury, not to water or other drinks

nodes.title: Classical Mechanics (Advanced)
nodes.goal: Lagrangians and Hamiltonians — mechanics made elegant.

quiz.prompt: A particle of mass m moves vertically with Lagrangian L = (1/2)mv^2 - mgx, where x is measured upward. Apply the Euler-Lagrange equation d/dt(dL/dv) = dL/dx. What equation of motion comes out?
quiz.answer: m dv/dt = -mg: free fall with acceleration g downward.
quiz.explain: dL/dv = mv, so the left-hand side is m dv/dt; dL/dx = -mg. The equation is therefore m dv/dt = -mg, ordinary free fall. Having no explicit time dependence conserves the Hamiltonian; it does not make the acceleration vanish.
choices: m dv/dt = +mg, since a potential always enters with a plus sign.
mv = -mgx, from setting the two partial derivatives equal.
m dv/dt = -mg: free fall with acceleration g downward.
dv/dt = 0, because L carries no explicit dependence on time.

quiz.prompt: A mass on a spring has L = (1/2)m x-dot squared - (1/2)k x squared, and the Hamiltonian built from it is H = p squared over 2m + (1/2)k x squared. As the mass oscillates, what happens to the values of H and of L?
quiz.answer: H stays constant while L varies through the cycle.
quiz.explain: H = T + V is the conserved total energy. L = T - V is not conserved: at the turning points L = -(1/2)k x squared and at the centre L = +(1/2)m x-dot squared, so it swings between the two. Energy moving between the stores leaves only the sum fixed.
choices: Both stay constant, since the system is isolated.
L stays constant while H varies through the cycle.
Both vary, since energy moves between kinetic and potential.
H stays constant while L varies through the cycle.

quiz.prompt: A double pendulum swings in a vertical plane: two rigid rods, two point bobs, all motion in that plane. How many generalized coordinates does a Lagrangian description need, and why?
quiz.answer: Two: the rods fix both lengths, leaving two angles free.
quiz.explain: Two point masses in a plane start with four coordinates; each rigid rod is one constraint and removes one, leaving two. The generalized coordinates are the two angles, and the constraint forces in the rods never appear.
choices: Four: each bob carries an x and a y coordinate of its own.
Two: the rods fix both lengths, leaving two angles free.
One: the pair swings together as a single rigid object.
Three: two angles and the length between the two bobs.

quiz.prompt: For a simple pendulum of length 2.45 m the Lagrangian gives the small-angle equation of motion theta-double-dot = -(g/L) theta. Taking g = 9.8 m/s2, give the angular frequency in rad/s.
quiz.explain: omega = sqrt(g/L) = sqrt(9.8/2.45) = sqrt(4) = 2 rad/s, so the period is about 3.14 s.

quiz.prompt: A particle moves in a central potential V(r). Written in polar coordinates the Lagrangian contains r and r-dot and phi-dot, but no phi itself. State what that absence immediately buys you.
quiz.answer: Angular momentum, the momentum conjugate to phi, is conserved.
choices: Angular momentum, the momentum conjugate to phi, is conserved.
The radial coordinate r must stay fixed throughout the motion.
The speed of the particle stays constant along the whole orbit.
The orbit closes on itself after exactly one revolution.
quiz.explain: A coordinate absent from the Lagrangian is cyclic, so the time derivative of its conjugate momentum is zero. Here that momentum is the angular momentum. The radius and the speed both still vary, and only special potentials give closed orbits.

quiz.prompt: Two students attack the same bead-on-a-rotating-hoop problem. One writes Newton's laws and must find the hoop's constraint force; the other writes a Lagrangian in the single coordinate theta. Compare the labour involved.
quiz.answer: The Lagrangian route never needs the constraint force.
choices: The Newtonian route alone can give the true motion.
The Lagrangian route must resolve each force vector.
Both routes require the constraint force to be found.
The Lagrangian route never needs the constraint force.
quiz.explain: Generalised coordinates already respect the constraint, so forces of constraint do no virtual work and drop out. That is the practical payoff of the Lagrangian formulation.

quiz.prompt: A block slides on a frictionless incline of 30 degrees, and the Lagrangian gives acceleration g sin(theta) along the slope. With g = 9.8 m/s squared, what is that acceleration, in m/s squared?
quiz.explain: sin 30 degrees = 0.5, so a = 9.8 x 0.5 = 4.9 m/s squared.

quiz.prompt: A free particle of mass 0.50 kg moves in one dimension at 4.0 m/s, so its Hamiltonian equals the kinetic energy. What value, in joules, does the Hamiltonian take?
quiz.explain: H = p squared over 2m = half x 0.50 x 16 = 4.0 J.

quiz.prompt: A bead slides on a frictionless wire bent into a fixed shape. Working in Cartesian coordinates gives two coupled equations plus an unknown constraint force. What does switching to arc length along the wire as the generalized coordinate buy you?
quiz.answer: One equation, with the constraint force gone.
choices: One equation, with the constraint force gone.
A faster numerical solution of the same two equations.
The constraint force written out explicitly, ready to read off.
Conservation of energy, which the Cartesian version lacked.
quiz.explain: Generalized coordinates that already satisfy the constraint reduce the number of equations and remove the workless constraint force from them.

quiz.prompt: A double pendulum's Lagrangian carries no explicit time dependence, but it does depend on both angles. Which conservation statement holds?
quiz.answer: Energy is conserved, and neither angular momentum is.
choices: Energy is conserved, and neither angular momentum is.
Both the energy and the total angular momentum are conserved.
Angular momentum is conserved but the energy is not.
Nothing at all is conserved, because the motion is chaotic.
quiz.explain: No explicit time dependence gives a conserved Hamiltonian; the angles appear in the Lagrangian, so their conjugate momenta are not conserved. Chaos does not repeal conservation laws.

lesson_media.alt: Trial trajectories approach a stationary-action path beside closed constant-Hamiltonian orbits in phase space.
lesson_media.caption: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian views encode the same dynamics while exposing different constraints and conserved structure.

lesson_media.title: Hamiltonian Motion Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change the trial path and inspect action alongside the phase-space trajectory.

nodes.title: Electrodynamics
nodes.goal: Maxwell's equations and electromagnetic waves.

quiz.prompt: Gauss's law for magnetism says the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. A student wraps a closed surface tightly around the north half of a bar magnet, cutting through the middle of the bar. What flux does that surface enclose?
quiz.answer: Zero: as much flux enters through the cut as leaves the pole.
quiz.explain: Inside the magnet the field lines run from south to north, so every line leaving the pole is matched by a line crossing the cut on its way in. Div B = 0 makes the total zero for any closed surface, whatever the strength: that is the statement that no magnetic monopole has ever been found.
choices: A positive flux, since only the north pole sits inside it.
A positive flux that dwindles to zero as the surface is widened out.
Zero, but only because a bar magnet is a fairly weak source.
Zero: as much flux enters through the cut as leaves the pole.

quiz.prompt: Maxwell's equations give the speed of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum as c = 1/sqrt(mu-nought times epsilon-nought). Suppose a future measurement found epsilon-nought to be four times its accepted value, with mu-nought unchanged. What would the predicted speed become?
quiz.answer: Half its present value.
quiz.explain: c varies as one over the square root of epsilon-nought, so multiplying epsilon-nought by four divides c by two. Nothing else enters: not the frequency, not the source, not the observer's motion.
choices: Twice its present value.
Half its present value.
Four times its present value.
Unchanged: c does not depend on those constants.

quiz.prompt: A plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum travels along +z. At one instant its electric field at the origin points along +x. Where does its magnetic field point at that same instant?
quiz.answer: Along +y, so that E cross B points along +z.
quiz.explain: The wave is transverse, and E, B and the direction of travel form a right-handed set with E and B in phase. E along +x with travel along +z therefore puts B along +y. Nothing oscillates along the direction of travel, and there is no quarter-cycle lag.
choices: Along +z, in the direction the wave is travelling.
Along +y, so that E cross B points along +z.
Along +x, in step with the electric field.
Along -y, a quarter cycle behind the electric field.

quiz.prompt: A plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum has an electric field amplitude of 600 V/m. Using B = E/c with c = 3.0e8 m/s, give the magnetic field amplitude in microtesla.
quiz.explain: B = 600 / 3.0e8 = 2.0e-6 T, that is 2 microtesla. The magnetic amplitude is always tiny in SI units, which is why E dominates the force on slow charges.

quiz.prompt: A student applies Ampere's law to a charging parallel-plate capacitor, choosing a surface that bulges between the plates where no conduction current crosses. She gets zero magnetic field, contradicting the answer from a surface cutting the wire. Diagnose the error.
quiz.answer: She left out the displacement current from the changing field.
choices: Ampere's law does not hold while a capacitor is charging up.
She left out the displacement current from the changing field.
The two surfaces must share the same boundary curve to compare.
The magnetic field between the plates really is exactly zero.
quiz.explain: Maxwell's added term, epsilon-nought times the rate of change of electric flux, supplies exactly what the missing conduction current would have. With it the law gives the same answer for every surface sharing the loop, and the field between the plates is not zero.

quiz.prompt: An antenna radiates into empty space. In the far field the E and B amplitudes fall as 1/r while the intensity falls as 1/r-squared. Explain why the total power crossing a sphere is the same at every radius.
quiz.answer: The area of the sphere grows exactly as fast as the intensity falls.
choices: The wave draws fresh energy out of the vacuum as it spreads.
The frequency falls with distance, so the intensity is conserved.
Energy is stored in the near field and released further out.
The area of the sphere grows exactly as fast as the intensity falls.
quiz.explain: Power is intensity times area. Intensity falls as 1/r-squared while the sphere grows as 4 pi r-squared, so the product is the same at every radius and nothing is lost in transit. The frequency of a wave in vacuum does not change with distance.

quiz.prompt: A parallel-plate capacitor is being charged by a steady conduction current of 5.0 A. What displacement current, in amperes, flows between its plates?
quiz.explain: Continuity requires the displacement current between the plates to match the conduction current in the wire, 5.0 A.

quiz.prompt: An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has a frequency of 5.0e14 Hz. Taking c = 3.0e8 m/s, what is its wavelength, in nanometres?
quiz.explain: lambda = c/f = 3.0e8 / 5.0e14 = 6.0e-7 m, which is 600 nm.

quiz.prompt: A coaxial cable carries a steady current out along the inner core and back along the outer sheath. A student predicts a strong magnetic field in the room around the cable. Using Ampere's law, correct them.
quiz.answer: The enclosed currents cancel, so the field outside is essentially zero.
choices: The field outside is doubled, since the two currents add up.
The field outside falls off as one over r squared instead of one over r.
The field outside appears only while the current is changing.
The enclosed currents cancel, so the field outside is essentially zero.
quiz.explain: A loop drawn outside the cable encloses equal and opposite currents, so the line integral of B, and hence the external field, vanishes.

quiz.prompt: An antenna is fed a perfectly steady direct current. What radiation should you expect from it?
quiz.answer: Almost none: radiating needs accelerating charge.
choices: Almost none: radiating needs accelerating charge.
Strong radiation, since any current makes a magnetic field.
Radiation at zero frequency, spreading out in the usual way.
Radiation along the antenna's axis, where the field vanishes.
quiz.explain: A steady current gives static fields. Radiation requires charges to accelerate, which is why antennas are driven with alternating current.

lesson_media.alt: A capacitor-gap top view shows changing through-page electric flux and circular magnetic field beside an orthogonal electromagnetic wave.
lesson_media.caption: Maxwell's displacement current completes Ampere's law; electromagnetic fields propagate mutually perpendicular to each other and travel.

lesson_media.title: Electromagnetic Wave Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change frequency while wavelength adjusts to preserve electromagnetic wave speed.

nodes.title: Quantum Mechanics
nodes.goal: The Schrödinger equation, spin, and measurement.

quiz.prompt: A wavefunction gives the value of |psi| squared near point A as twice its value near point B. Many identically prepared particles then have their positions measured. What should you expect?
quiz.answer: About twice as many detections near A as near B.
quiz.explain: Born's rule makes |psi| squared a probability density: it says how often a detection lands in a region, not where any one particle sits and not how much of a particle is there. Each electron is always found whole, at a single place.
choices: Every particle detected at A, since |psi| squared is larger there.
Each particle found smeared out, with more of it sitting at A.
Equal numbers at A and B, since |psi| squared fixes energy.
About twice as many detections near A as near B.

quiz.prompt: An electron sits in the ground state of a one-dimensional infinite square well. The well is then widened to twice its original length. What happens to the ground-state energy?
quiz.answer: It falls to a quarter of its old value.
quiz.explain: The levels go as n squared over L squared, so doubling L divides every level by four. Widening a well always lowers its levels and packs them closer together, which is why a large box behaves almost classically.
choices: It falls to half its old value.
It doubles, since the electron now has more room to move.
It is unchanged, since the width does not enter the energy.
It falls to a quarter of its old value.

quiz.prompt: A measurement of an electron's spin along the z-axis gives 'up'. If you immediately measure spin along the x-axis, the result is...
quiz.answer: equally likely to be x-up or x-down, a 50/50 outcome.
quiz.explain: Since spin-x and spin-z are incompatible observables, a z-up state is an equal superposition of x-up and x-down, giving 50/50 outcomes.
choices: equally likely to be x-up or x-down, a 50/50 outcome.
certain to be x-down, the opposite of the z result.
certain to be x-up, matching the previous z-up result.
always zero, since the spin along x has no value.

quiz.prompt: An electron trapped in a one-dimensional infinite square well has a ground-state energy of 2.0 eV. Give the energy of the n = 3 level, in eV.
quiz.explain: Levels scale as n-squared, so E3 = 9 x E1 = 9 x 2.0 = 18 eV.

quiz.prompt: Silver atoms pass a z-oriented Stern-Gerlach magnet; the z-up beam then enters an x-oriented magnet, and the x-up output enters a second z-magnet. Predict what leaves that final z-magnet.
quiz.answer: Half emerge z-up and half z-down.
choices: The whole beam emerges z-up, as it did before.
The whole beam emerges z-down, flipped by the x-magnet.
Half emerge z-up and half z-down.
Nothing emerges, since the state has been destroyed.
quiz.explain: Measuring x destroys the earlier z information, because the spin operators do not commute. The x-up state is an equal superposition of z-up and z-down.

quiz.prompt: A student claims the uncertainty principle is mere clumsiness: with better instruments one could pin down a particle's position and momentum together as sharply as one liked. Assess the claim.
quiz.answer: Wrong: the spread belongs to the quantum state, not to the apparatus.
choices: Right; today's detectors are simply not yet precise enough for it.
Right, since any measurement necessarily disturbs the system.
Wrong, because momentum means nothing for a spread-out wave.
Wrong: the spread belongs to the quantum state, not to the apparatus.
quiz.explain: The position and momentum wavefunctions are Fourier transforms of one another, so narrowing one widens the other. That is a property of the state, which no instrument can evade, and it is distinct from the separate fact that measuring disturbs.

quiz.prompt: An electron in a one-dimensional infinite square well has a ground-state energy of 1.5 eV. What is the energy, in eV, of the n = 4 level?
quiz.explain: Levels scale as n squared, so E4 = 16 x 1.5 = 24 eV.

quiz.prompt: A photon's energy in electronvolts is 1240 divided by its wavelength in nanometres. What is the energy, in eV, of a 500 nm photon?
A researcher prepares many electrons in the same superposition, measures each one once, and gets a scatter of results. She concludes her preparation was sloppy. Diagnose the error in that conclusion.
quiz.answer: Identically prepared states can still give a spread of results each time.
choices: The apparatus must be drifting out of calibration between the runs.
Identically prepared states can still give a spread of results each time.
Each electron carried a hidden value fixed before it was measured.
The electrons must have interacted with each other during the run.
quiz.explain: Measuring a superposition is probabilistic, so a scatter is exactly what a perfectly prepared ensemble gives. The spread is the physics, not a fault in the preparation, and Bell tests rule out a pre-existing hidden value behind it.

quiz.prompt: A particle meets a barrier taller than its energy, and yet a detector on the far side clicks from time to time. Which account fits?
quiz.answer: Its wavefunction decays inside the barrier without reaching zero.
choices: A few of the particles happen to arrive carrying more energy than the rest.
The barrier momentarily drops, letting particles slip across.
Its wavefunction decays inside the barrier without reaching zero.
The detector is picking up the reflected particles instead.
quiz.explain: Inside a barrier the solution is an exponential decay rather than an oscillation, so a small amplitude survives to the far side and the transmission probability is non-zero. No particle borrows energy and no barrier flickers.

lesson_media.alt: A scaled signed wavefunction and relative squared-magnitude shape are compared with repeated position detections.
lesson_media.caption: The state supplies amplitudes; the normalized squared magnitude predicts the distribution of measurement outcomes.

lesson_media.title: Quantum Sampling Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Choose a state and draw a reproducible seeded mock sample from its predicted probability distribution.

nodes.title: Statistical Mechanics
nodes.goal: From atoms to temperature: entropy as counting.

quiz.prompt: Boltzmann's relation S = k ln W connects entropy to W, the number of microstates. If system A has twice as many accessible microstates as system B, then compared with B, system A's entropy is...
quiz.answer: greater by k ln 2.
quiz.explain: S_A − S_B = k ln(2W) − k ln(W) = k ln 2, so the entropy differs by k ln 2.
choices: unchanged, since entropy depends only on energy.
twice as large.
smaller by k ln 2.
greater by k ln 2.

quiz.prompt: In the Boltzmann distribution, the ratio of populations of two states at temperature T depends on their energy gap ΔE as e^(−ΔE/kT). As the temperature increases toward very high values, the population of the higher-energy state relative to the lower one...
quiz.answer: approaches equality with that of the lower state.
quiz.explain: As T → ∞, ΔE/kT → 0 and e^(−ΔE/kT) → 1, so the two states become nearly equally populated.
choices: approaches equality with that of the lower state.
becomes exactly equal to the ratio ΔE/kT.
drops steadily toward zero as T increases.
exceeds the lower state without any bound.

quiz.prompt: Two macrostates of the same isolated system have W1 = 10^20 and W2 = 10^22 accessible microstates, and every microstate is equally likely. Which statement follows?
quiz.answer: The system spends about a hundred times longer in the second.
quiz.explain: Equal likelihood per microstate makes the chance of a macrostate proportional to its microstate count, so a factor of 100 in W is a factor of 100 in time spent. Entropy is k ln W, so the entropies differ by k ln 100, about 4.6k — not by a factor of a hundred.
choices: The second has an entropy a hundred times larger than the first.
The system spends about a hundred times longer in the second.
The two are equally likely, since both counts are enormous.
The first is favoured, since lower entropy is more stable.

quiz.prompt: A two-level system has an energy gap equal to kT at temperature T. Using the Boltzmann factor exp(-dE/kT), give the ratio of upper-state to lower-state population, to three decimal places.
quiz.explain: exp(-1) = 0.3679. When the gap matches the thermal energy the upper level is about a third as populated as the lower.

quiz.prompt: Four distinguishable coins are tossed and the macrostate is taken to be the number of heads. Explain why two heads shows up far more often than four heads.
quiz.answer: Six microstates give two heads, but only one gives four.
choices: Two heads costs the four coins less energy than four heads.
The coins interact and prefer to balance one another out.
Four heads is forbidden outright by the second law.
Six microstates give two heads, but only one gives four.
quiz.explain: Every one of the sixteen microstates is equally likely, and six of them show two heads against one showing four. The macrostate with the most microstates wins by counting alone: no energy and no law of thermodynamics is involved.

quiz.prompt: An ideal gas expands freely into the evacuated half of an insulated box. No heat enters and no work is done, and the gas never crowds back into one half. Identify what has changed.
quiz.answer: The entropy rose along with the volume now accessible.
choices: The internal energy fell as the gas spread out.
The entropy rose along with the volume now accessible.
The temperature dropped because work was done.
The total energy leaked away into the vacuum region.
quiz.explain: With Q = 0 and W = 0 the internal energy and temperature are unchanged, but each molecule now has twice the volume, so W and hence the entropy increase.

quiz.prompt: A system has 8 equally likely microstates. Using S = k ln W, what is the value of S divided by k? Give three decimal places.
Three distinguishable coins are tossed. How many microstates give exactly one head?
quiz.explain: The single head can be on any one of the three coins, giving 3 microstates.

quiz.prompt: A colleague argues that a gas could spontaneously crowd into one half of a room, so the second law is only statistical. How should you reply?
quiz.answer: True in principle, but the odds are unimaginably small.
choices: False: such an arrangement has no microstates available to it.
True in principle, but the odds are unimaginably small.
False: the second law forbids it exactly, at any system size.
True, and rooms are small enough to see it now and then.
quiz.explain: The arrangement is allowed and does have microstates, but its share of them falls as 2 to the power of minus N. For a roomful of about 10^25 molecules that probability is far beyond ever being seen, which is why the statistical law looks absolute.

quiz.prompt: Two identical blocks at different temperatures are placed in contact inside an isolated container. What happens to the combined entropy while heat flows?
quiz.answer: It rises: the cold block gains more than the hot one loses.
choices: It falls, because the two temperatures are becoming uniform.
It rises: the cold block gains more than the hot one loses.
It stays fixed, since the energy is merely being transferred.
It rises only if the two blocks differ in heat capacity.
quiz.explain: The same heat dQ changes entropy by dQ/T, which is larger where T is smaller. The cold block therefore gains more than the hot block loses and the total rises, whatever the heat capacities, even though the energy is only moved about.

lesson_media.alt: Sixteen four-coin microstates produce the one-four-six-four-one multiplicity distribution over macrostates.
lesson_media.caption: Entropy grows with multiplicity, making the balanced macrostate most probable without making any microstate more likely.

lesson_media.title: Microstate Counter
lesson_media.instructions: Choose the number of heads and compare macrostate multiplicity with entropy.

nodes.title: Relativity
nodes.goal: Special relativity rigorously; general relativity's ideas.

quiz.prompt: A muon has a proper lifetime of 2.0 microseconds. It travels at a speed where the Lorentz factor γ = 5. In the lab frame, how many microseconds does it live before decaying?
quiz.explain: Time dilation gives the lab-frame lifetime as γ times the proper time: 5 × 2.0 µs = 10 µs.

quiz.prompt: An atomic clock at the foot of a tall tower and an identical clock at the top are compared after a year. Which one has ticked ahead, and why?
quiz.answer: The top clock: it sits higher in the gravitational potential.
quiz.explain: Clocks deeper in a gravitational potential tick more slowly as seen from higher up, so the top clock gains — about a third of a microsecond a year over a 100 m tower, and the effect has been measured over a single metre. The tower top does move slightly faster as Earth turns, but that would make it lose, and it is some hundreds of times smaller.
choices: The foot clock: it is deeper in the field and so runs faster.
The top clock: it sits higher in the gravitational potential.
Neither: gravitational time dilation needs a black hole to show.
The top clock, but only because Earth's spin carries it faster.

quiz.prompt: An astronaut is sealed in a small windowless capsule and feels a steady 9.8 newtons per kilogram pressing her to the floor. What can experiments done entirely inside the capsule tell her?
quiz.answer: Nothing that tells gravity apart from steady acceleration.
quiz.explain: The equivalence principle says a uniform gravitational field and a uniformly accelerating frame are locally indistinguishable, and both balls fall together either way. Only tidal effects — the slight convergence of a real planet's field across the capsule — would betray it, and that is what the word 'locally' sets aside.
choices: Nothing that tells gravity apart from steady acceleration.
That she must be resting on the surface of a planet.
That she must be accelerating, since gravity is never felt.
She can separate the two by dropping two balls of different mass.

quiz.prompt: A rod of proper length 10.0 m flies past a laboratory at a speed for which the Lorentz factor is 2.5. Give the length the laboratory measures, in metres.
quiz.explain: Length contraction divides the proper length by gamma: 10.0 / 2.5 = 4.0 m.

quiz.prompt: A 20 m pole is carried at gamma = 2 through a 10 m barn. In the barn frame the contracted pole just fits with both doors briefly shut; in the pole frame the barn is only 5 m long and cannot possibly contain it. Resolve the apparent paradox.
quiz.answer: The frames disagree about which of the two doors shut first.
choices: The pole physically shrinks and stays shrunk after.
The frames disagree about which of the two doors shut first.
One of the two frames must simply be mistaken here.
The barn frame counts because the barn is at rest.
quiz.explain: Simultaneity is frame dependent. Events that are simultaneous in the barn frame are not in the pole frame, so in the pole frame the doors shut one after the other.

quiz.prompt: GPS satellites orbit fast and high. Their speed makes their clocks run slow by about 7 microseconds a day, while their higher gravitational potential makes them run fast by about 45. Say what the ground software must do.
quiz.answer: Correct for the net speed-up: the gravitational effect wins.
choices: Ignore both, since the gravitational and velocity effects cancel.
Apply the special-relativistic slowing on its own and stop there.
Run the satellite clocks faster to match the ground clocks.
Correct for the net speed-up: the gravitational effect wins.
quiz.explain: The two effects have opposite signs and do not cancel: 45 minus 7 leaves about +38 microseconds a day. Untreated, that would push positions kilometres out within a day. The correction is applied on the ground and in the satellite oscillator, not by speeding the clocks up to match.

quiz.prompt: A particle has a rest energy of 500 MeV and a total energy of 2500 MeV. What is its Lorentz factor?
quiz.explain: gamma = total energy / rest energy = 2500/500 = 5.

quiz.prompt: Two spaceships head towards each other, each at 0.5c relative to a station. Using relativistic velocity addition, what is their speed relative to one another, as a multiple of c?
A crew accelerates their ship steadily for many years and expects eventually to pass the speed of light. What does relativity predict instead?
quiz.answer: Their speed approaches c without ever reaching it.
choices: They pass c but cannot detect it from inside the ship.
Their speed approaches c without ever reaching it.
The engine fails once the ship's mass becomes infinite.
They reach c exactly, and at that instant time stops for them.
quiz.explain: Steady proper acceleration gives ever smaller gains in coordinate speed; the energy required diverges as v approaches c.

quiz.prompt: A ring laser on a rotating platform times light going each way around the loop and finds the two arrival times differ. A student claims this refutes the constancy of the speed of light. Correct them.
quiz.answer: In the rotating frame the two paths differ in length.
choices: Rotation genuinely alters the local speed of light in the loop.
In the rotating frame the two paths differ in length.
The clocks, rather than the light, are at fault in this setup.
Relativity simply does not apply to any rotating apparatus.
quiz.explain: The platform is not an inertial frame: while the light is in flight the beam splitter moves, so the co-rotating and counter-rotating beams cover unequal distances. Measured locally the speed of light is unchanged, which is why the Sagnac effect is used in navigation gyroscopes rather than treated as a refutation.

lesson_media.alt: A Minkowski light cone and barn-pole event diagram distinguish invariant causality from frame-dependent simultaneity.
lesson_media.caption: Observers share the interval and timelike causal order, while spacelike door-event order and simultaneity depend on frame.

lesson_media.title: Relativistic Frame Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change frame speed and proper time to compare coordinate time and simultaneity.

nodes.title: Solid State Physics
nodes.goal: Crystals, bands, semiconductors — why chips work.

quiz.prompt: Three crystalline solids are measured at room temperature: in the first the electron bands overlap, the second has a 1.1 eV gap and the third a 6 eV gap. Sort them into conductor, semiconductor and insulator.
quiz.answer: The overlap conducts, 1.1 eV is the semiconductor, 6 eV insulates.
quiz.explain: Overlapping bands leave carriers free with no gap to cross. A gap of about an electronvolt lets thermal energy promote a workable few, which is a semiconductor. Six electronvolts is hundreds of times the roughly 0.025 eV available at room temperature, so almost nothing crosses.
choices: Overlap insulates, 6 eV conducts: a wide gap means a big current.
All three conduct, since room temperature supplies ample energy.
6 eV is the semiconductor; 1.1 eV is too small a gap to matter.
The overlap conducts, 1.1 eV is the semiconductor, 6 eV insulates.

quiz.prompt: A silicon wafer is doped with phosphorus, which has five valence electrons, on one side and with boron, which has three, on the other. Which side has electrons as its majority carrier, and what is that side called?
quiz.answer: The phosphorus side, which is n-type.
quiz.explain: Phosphorus brings one valence electron more than the four bonds need, and the spare is free to move: n-type. Boron is one short and leaves a hole: p-type. The donor ion left behind is positive, but it is locked in the lattice and carries no current.
choices: The boron side, which is n-type.
The phosphorus side, but it is called p-type: donors are positive.
The phosphorus side, which is n-type.
Both sides equally, since doping adds electrons either way.

quiz.prompt: Unlike a metal, the electrical conductivity of a pure semiconductor generally increases as temperature rises. Why?
quiz.answer: A higher temperature lifts many more electrons across the band gap.
quiz.explain: What changes steeply with temperature is the number of carriers, not their speed: the population above the gap grows roughly exponentially. Warming actually increases lattice scattering, and the gap narrows only slightly, so the carrier count is what wins.
choices: Warming makes each electron move faster, so more current flows.
The lattice vibrations scatter the electrons less as it warms.
Higher temperature shrinks the band gap almost to nothing.
A higher temperature lifts many more electrons across the band gap.

quiz.prompt: A semiconductor has a band gap of 1.1 eV. Using photon energy in eV equal to 1240 divided by wavelength in nanometres, give the longest wavelength it can absorb, in nanometres, to the nearest nanometre.
quiz.explain: 1240 / 1.1 = 1127 nm, in the near infrared. Longer wavelengths carry too little energy per photon to lift an electron across the gap, which is why silicon looks opaque but passes infrared.

quiz.prompt: A silicon wafer is doped with boron, which has three valence electrons. A Hall-effect measurement then shows the majority carriers are positive. Explain the result.
quiz.answer: Boron leaves vacancies in the bonding, and holes carry the charge.
choices: Boron leaves vacancies in the bonding, and holes carry the charge.
The boron ions are positive and drift bodily through the lattice.
Boron donates a spare electron; the Hall sign convention flips it.
The magnetic field, not the carrier sign, sets the Hall sign.
quiz.explain: Each boron atom is one electron short of four bonds. Neighbouring electrons hop into the vacancy, so the vacancy itself travels and behaves as a positive carrier. The dopant atoms stay put, and the sign of the Hall voltage is set by the sign of the moving charge.

quiz.prompt: Cooling a copper wire from 300 K to 77 K lowers its resistance, while cooling a pure silicon sample the same way raises its resistance enormously. Account for the opposite trends.
quiz.answer: Copper's carrier count is fixed; silicon's must be excited.
choices: Copper's carrier count is fixed; silicon's must be excited.
Cooling slows copper's electrons, so they scatter less on the way.
Cooling shrinks copper's lattice, packing its electrons closer.
Copper's resistance comes from its electrons, silicon's from nuclei.
quiz.explain: A metal always has the same number of conduction electrons; cooling only calms the lattice vibrations that scatter them, so resistance falls. In a pure semiconductor the carriers must first be lifted across the gap by thermal energy, and cooling starves that supply, so resistance climbs.

quiz.prompt: A semiconductor has a band gap of 0.75 eV. Using photon energy in eV equal to 1240 divided by wavelength in nanometres, what is the longest wavelength it can absorb, in nanometres, to the nearest nanometre?
quiz.explain: 1240 / 0.75 = 1653.3 nm, so 1653 nm to the nearest nanometre.

quiz.prompt: A cubic crystal has a lattice constant of 0.40 nm. How many unit cells lie along an edge 1.0 micrometre long?
quiz.explain: 1.0 micrometre is 1000 nm, and 1000 / 0.40 = 2500 cells.

quiz.prompt: A pn junction is wired with its p-side to the negative terminal of a battery. What current should you expect?
quiz.answer: Very little: the junction is reverse biased.
choices: A large current, since a junction conducts either way round.
A current that grows steadily as the voltage is raised.
Very little: the junction is reverse biased.
No current until the metal contacts themselves break down.
quiz.explain: Reverse bias widens the depletion region, so only a tiny saturation current flows until breakdown.

quiz.prompt: An engineer finds a silicon sensor drifts badly as the laboratory warms, while a metal-film resistor barely moves. Explain the contrast.
quiz.answer: Silicon's carrier count climbs steeply with temperature.
choices: Silicon expands far more, changing the sensor's dimensions.
The metal film radiates its heat away much more quickly.
Silicon's carrier count climbs steeply with temperature.
Silicon's electrons scatter less as it warms, unlike the metal's.
quiz.explain: In a semiconductor the number of carriers is thermally activated across the gap and rises roughly exponentially, so its resistance is very temperature sensitive. A metal keeps its carrier count fixed and only its scattering changes, which is a mild, nearly linear effect.

lesson_media.alt: Energy-band diagrams compare a wide-gap insulator, thermally excited semiconductor, and donor-doped semiconductor.
lesson_media.caption: Conductivity follows available carriers and states; doping changes population without simply erasing the band gap.

lesson_media.title: Band and Carrier Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change band gap, temperature, and doping to inspect the carrier population.

nodes.title: Particle Physics
nodes.goal: Quarks, leptons and the Standard Model.

quiz.prompt: A proton is made of two up quarks and one down quark. Given the up quark has charge +2/3 and the down quark −1/3 (in units of the elementary charge), what is the proton's total charge?
quiz.explain: Summing the quark charges: (+2/3) + (+2/3) + (−1/3) = +1, the proton's charge.

quiz.prompt: The range of a force goes roughly as h-bar c divided by the mediator's rest energy. The weak force reaches only about 0.002 femtometres, while electromagnetism reaches across a room. What does that contrast say about the two mediators?
quiz.answer: The W and Z are heavy; the photon has no rest mass at all.
quiz.explain: Range and mediator mass are inversely related. With h-bar c = 197 MeV femtometres, an 80 GeV W gives about 0.002 fm, while a massless photon gives unlimited range. Strength and range are separate questions: the weak force is short-ranged because its carriers are heavy, not because it is weak.
choices: The W and Z are heavy; the photon has no rest mass at all.
The photon is heavy and the W and Z are light, hence the short reach.
Both are massless; the weak force is short-ranged because it is feeble.
The weak mediators decay en route, though both are massless.

quiz.prompt: A new particle is discovered that feels the weak and electromagnetic interactions, shows no strong interaction at all, and shows no sign of internal structure. How should it be classified?
quiz.answer: As a charged lepton.
quiz.explain: Leptons are the fundamental fermions that do not feel the strong force; a charged one also feels electromagnetism. Hadrons are built from quarks and do feel the strong force, and a baryon is one kind of hadron. Feeling a force is not the same as carrying it.
choices: As a hadron, since it feels more than one force.
As a baryon, since it is a fundamental particle.
As a gauge boson, since it carries the weak force.
As a charged lepton.

quiz.prompt: A neutral pion at rest, with a rest energy of 135 MeV, decays into two photons. Give the energy of each photon, in MeV.
quiz.explain: Momentum conservation sends the photons back to back with equal energy, so each takes half the rest energy: 135/2 = 67.5 MeV.

quiz.prompt: A detector records many neutron decays into a proton and an electron. The electron energy varies continuously from event to event rather than taking one fixed value. Say what this implies.
quiz.answer: A third, unseen particle shares the energy.
choices: Energy conservation fails in weak decays.
A third, unseen particle shares the energy.
The neutron mass differs from event to event.
The electron loses energy in the detector walls.
quiz.explain: A two-body decay from rest fixes each energy. The continuous spectrum was Pauli's reason for proposing the neutrino, later confirmed directly.

quiz.prompt: A student writes free-neutron decay as n going to p plus an electron. Charge balances and baryon number balances. Evaluate the equation as written.
quiz.answer: It fails lepton number: an electron antineutrino must go too.
choices: It is fine as written; nothing at all is missing.
It fails because the momentum cannot balance.
It fails lepton number: an electron antineutrino must go too.
It fails because the electron is much too light.
quiz.explain: The left side has lepton number zero and the electron carries +1, so an antineutrino with -1 is required. That is also why the electron energy spectrum is continuous.

quiz.prompt: A neutron holds one up quark of charge +2/3 and two down quarks of charge -1/3 each. What is its total charge, in units of the elementary charge?
quiz.explain: 2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0, so the neutron is neutral.

quiz.prompt: A particle of rest energy 91.2 GeV decays while at rest. What total energy, in GeV, do its decay products carry away?
quiz.explain: Energy is conserved, so the products share exactly the parent's rest energy, 91.2 GeV.

quiz.prompt: A detector records a curving track that stops in the electromagnetic calorimeter and deposits its energy in a characteristic shower. Which identification fits best?
quiz.answer: An electron or positron.
choices: A neutrino, which leaves no track at all.
A neutron, which is neutral and passes through.
A muon, which punches on through the calorimeter.
An electron or positron.
quiz.explain: A charged track that showers and stops in the electromagnetic calorimeter is the signature of an electron or positron.

quiz.prompt: Someone proposes a decay in which a proton turns into a positron and a neutrino. Which conservation law does this break?
quiz.answer: Baryon number.
choices: Electric charge.
Energy and momentum together.
Lepton number, with everything else balancing.
Baryon number.
quiz.explain: Charge (+1 to +1) and lepton number (0 to -1 + 1 = 0) both balance, and the decay is energetically allowed; only baryon number, 1 to 0, fails.
