lesson_media.alt: Quark charges add to proton and neutron charges beside a beta-decay ledger for three conserved quantum numbers.
lesson_media.caption: Allowed composite particles and decay channels satisfy additive charge, baryon-number, and lepton-number constraints.

lesson_media.title: Decay Conservation Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Choose a candidate decay channel and audit its conserved quantum numbers.

nodes.title: The Art of Experiment
nodes.goal: Uncertainty, error analysis, and how physics is actually tested.

quiz.prompt: Two independent measurements are added: x = 3.0 ± 0.3 and y = 4.0 ± 0.4, with independent random uncertainties combined in quadrature. What is the uncertainty in x + y? Give your answer to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: For a sum of independent quantities, uncertainties add in quadrature: √(0.3² + 0.4²) = √0.25 = 0.5.

quiz.prompt: A voltmeter reads 0.20 V high on every reading, because it was never zeroed. A student measures a cell on open circuit as 1.52 V and again under load as 1.28 V, and reports the drop as the difference between them. How is that reported drop affected?
quiz.answer: Not at all: a constant offset cancels in the difference.
quiz.explain: Both readings are 0.20 V high, so the offset subtracts away: 1.52 - 1.28 = 0.24 V, the same as the true 1.32 - 1.08. That is why differences and gradients often survive an uncalibrated instrument. A systematic offset shifts readings; it does not scatter them.
choices: It is 0.40 V too large, since both readings are shifted.
It is 0.20 V too large, since each reading carries the offset.
It becomes uncertain, since the offset scatters the readings.
Not at all: a constant offset cancels in the difference.

quiz.prompt: A student takes many repeated readings of the same quantity and averages them. This procedure most directly reduces the effect of...
quiz.answer: Random errors, since they tend to cancel when averaged.
quiz.explain: Averaging n readings shrinks random scatter by the square root of n, because the fluctuations fall on both sides of the true value. A fixed offset falls on one side every time, so it survives the average untouched however many readings are taken.
choices: Random errors, since they tend to cancel when averaged.
Systematic errors, since those also cancel out when averaged.
The instrument's fixed calibration offset in each reading.
Every kind of error at once, given enough repeated readings.

quiz.prompt: A pendulum period is measured as 2.00 s with a 1.0 percent uncertainty, and g is obtained from a relation in which g varies as 1 over T squared. Give the percentage uncertainty in g.
quiz.explain: For a power law the fractional uncertainties multiply by the exponent, so a 1.0 percent error in T gives 2.0 percent in g.

quiz.prompt: A team reports a new particle at 3.1 standard deviations above background, while a rival team using a comparable detector sees nothing there. Advise on how to read the situation.
quiz.answer: Suggestive, not decisive: more data and an independent check.
choices: Three sigma settles it, so the rival team must have blundered.
The claim should be discarded straight away as a fluctuation.
Suggestive, not decisive: more data and an independent check.
Statistics cannot settle a question of physics either way.
quiz.explain: Three-sigma excesses are common once many channels are searched, and most have faded with more data. Neither believing nor discarding it is warranted: particle physics reserves discovery for five sigma plus an independent confirmation.

quiz.prompt: Two laboratories measure the same constant. Lab A reports 1.652 plus or minus 0.001 and lab B reports 1.641 plus or minus 0.002, so the stated intervals do not overlap. Give the most likely explanation.
quiz.answer: An unrecognised systematic error in at least one of the labs.
choices: An unrecognised systematic error in at least one of the labs.
One lab must have made an arithmetic slip somewhere.
Random noise happened to be large in both data sets.
The constant itself differs between the two locations.
quiz.explain: Quoted errors here are statistical. A gap of five combined sigma normally means an uncorrected instrumental or method bias, not bad luck in the noise.

quiz.prompt: Five readings of one quantity are 4.8, 5.0, 5.1, 4.9 and 5.2. What is their mean?
quiz.explain: The five values sum to 25.0, and 25.0/5 = 5.0.

quiz.prompt: A length carries a 1.0 percent uncertainty and a time carries 2.0 percent. For speed = length / time, what is the percentage uncertainty in the speed?
quiz.explain: For a quotient, fractional uncertainties add: 1.0 + 2.0 = 3.0 percent.

quiz.prompt: A group fits a model to 40 data points and obtains a reduced chi-squared of 0.02. What should they suspect first?
quiz.answer: Their quoted uncertainties are far too large for the data.
choices: The model captures the physics unusually well.
There are too few data points for a meaningful fit.
A systematic shift has moved every point in step.
Their quoted uncertainties are far too large for the data.
quiz.explain: Reduced chi-squared measures how well a model's predictions match the data relative to the claimed uncertainties: sum the squared residuals (each data point's distance from the model, divided by its own error bar), then divide by the degrees of freedom. A good fit lands near 1 — the residuals are about as large as the error bars say they should be. A value as low as 0.02 means the residuals are far SMALLER than the error bars claim, which usually points to overstated uncertainties rather than an unusually perfect fit.

quiz.prompt: A student averages 400 readings, achieving excellent precision, yet the result sits ten standard errors from the accepted value. What is the likely explanation?
quiz.answer: An uncorrected systematic error.
choices: Bad luck: ten sigma comes up occasionally.
An uncorrected systematic error.
Too few readings to beat the random scatter.
The accepted value itself must simply be wrong.
quiz.explain: Averaging beats down random error but does nothing to a systematic offset, which then dominates and shows up as a large, precise discrepancy.

lesson_media.alt: Repeated readings contrast random scatter and systematic bias beside a calibration fit with residuals and an outlier.
lesson_media.caption: A sound experiment separates imprecision from bias, calibrates its scale, and tests residual structure rather than appearance.

lesson_media.title: Measurement Error Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change scatter, calibration offset, and outliers to inspect residuals and uncertainty.

nodes.title: Quantum Field Theory
nodes.goal: Fields as the deepest known description of matter.

quiz.prompt: Every electron ever measured has exactly the same mass and the same charge, to the limits of experiment. How does quantum field theory account for that exact sameness?
quiz.answer: All electrons are excitations of one and the same field.
quiz.explain: There is one electron field filling space, and an electron is a quantum of it. Two quanta of the same field can no more differ in mass or charge than two ripples can differ in what the pond is made of. That strict identity is also what forces Fermi statistics on them.
choices: All electrons are excitations of one and the same field.
They were all produced in the Big Bang by a single process.
Small differences do exist, below present measuring precision.
Each electron has its own field, and the fields happen to match.

quiz.prompt: In electron-electron scattering the internal photon line of a Feynman diagram carries an energy and momentum that need not satisfy E squared = p squared c squared. A student concludes such a photon should be detectable as an unusual particle. Correct them.
quiz.answer: Internal lines are summed over and never reach the final state.
quiz.explain: An internal line is a term in a calculation, integrated over every energy and momentum it could carry; only external lines match particles that enter or leave. Every photon that is actually detected is on shell.
choices: Internal lines are summed over and never reach the final state.
The relation always holds, so the student's premise is mistaken.
It is detectable, but only within the collision region itself.
It is an ordinary photon; the relation fails for all photons.

quiz.prompt: The Dirac equation's solutions come in positive- and negative-energy pairs, and the theory is made consistent by reading the negative-energy ones as antiparticles. A new charged fundamental fermion is then discovered. What does that argument predict for it?
quiz.answer: A partner of equal mass and opposite charge must exist.
quiz.explain: The pairing follows from combining special relativity with quantum mechanics, so it applies to every charged fermion, quark or lepton alike. Masses are positive for both members; it is charge and the other additive quantum numbers that reverse.
choices: A partner of opposite mass and equal charge must exist.
No partner is needed unless the new particle is a lepton.
A partner of equal mass and opposite charge must exist.
A partner exists only if it is its own antiparticle.

quiz.prompt: The Compton wavelength h/(mc) of the electron is 2.43e-12 m. A hypothetical particle has exactly 100 times the electron mass. Give its Compton wavelength in units of 1e-14 m.
quiz.explain: The Compton wavelength is inversely proportional to mass: 2.43e-12 / 100 = 2.43e-14 m. It sets the scale below which pair creation makes single-particle language fail.

quiz.prompt: A student computes the one-loop correction to the electron self-energy and the integral diverges. Describe how quantum field theory deals with this.
quiz.answer: The divergence is absorbed into the measured parameters of the theory.
choices: The theory has to be abandoned as internally inconsistent.
The offending diagram is discarded by hand and forgotten.
The integral is cut off at the Planck scale and the rest ignored.
The divergence is absorbed into the measured parameters of the theory.
quiz.explain: The bare mass and charge are not observable. Rewriting every prediction in terms of the measured values soaks up the infinities and leaves finite relations between observables, such as the electron's anomalous magnetic moment.

quiz.prompt: Two neutral, uncharged conducting plates a micrometre apart, in a region emptied of particles, are pushed together. A student objects that with nothing between the plates there is nothing to do the pushing. Where does the objection go wrong?
quiz.answer: Empty space still has field modes, and fewer of them fit inside.
choices: Empty space still has field modes, and fewer of them fit inside.
A thin residual gas always remains, and it presses them together.
The plates attract gravitationally, which is what is measured.
The objection stands; the measured force is stray surface charge.
quiz.explain: The quantum vacuum is empty of particles but not of fields. The gap admits only a restricted set of electromagnetic modes while the outside admits all of them, so the zero-point energy density is lower between the plates and they are pushed together. That is the Casimir force, measured against the prediction to a few percent.

quiz.prompt: A tree-level rate receives a correction of relative size alpha, about 1/137. By what percentage does that shift the rate? Give one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 1/137 = 0.0073, that is roughly 0.7 percent.

quiz.prompt: A force's range is h-bar c divided by the mediator's rest energy. With h-bar c = 197 MeV femtometres and a mediator of rest energy 197 MeV, what is the range, in femtometres?
quiz.explain: 197 / 197 = 1 femtometre.

quiz.prompt: The electron's magnetic moment is measured to twelve digits and sits slightly above the value Dirac's equation alone gives. How does quantum field theory account for the difference?
quiz.answer: Loop corrections from virtual particles alter the interaction vertex.
choices: The electron has a small internal size that Dirac neglected.
Relativistic corrections to the electron's orbit were dropped.
Loop corrections from virtual particles alter the interaction vertex.
The applied field polarises the electron's own spin slightly.
quiz.explain: Dirac gives g exactly 2 for a structureless spin-half particle. Radiative corrections, computed as loop diagrams, add about one part in a thousand, and the calculation agrees with experiment to twelve digits — evidence that the electron is still pointlike.

quiz.prompt: A student computing a scattering rate finds the answer depends on the arbitrary cut-off imposed on loop momenta and concludes the theory is meaningless. What is the standard reply?
quiz.answer: Re-express predictions in measured quantities and it drops out.
choices: The cut-off is a physical scale, so the dependence is real.
Re-express predictions in measured quantities and it drops out.
Loop diagrams should simply be discarded as unphysical artefacts.
Only the tree-level term ever carries any physical meaning.
quiz.explain: Renormalisation absorbs the cut-off dependence into a handful of measured parameters. Relations between observables then come out finite and independent of the cut-off, which is what makes the loop terms predictive rather than disposable.

lesson_media.alt: One bosonic spatial mode sits above occupation-number energy levels beside a Feynman contribution with external and internal lines.
lesson_media.caption: For a bosonic mode, occupation sets quantized energy rather than classical field amplitude; diagram lines organize amplitudes, not photographed trajectories.

lesson_media.title: Field Mode Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change one free bosonic mode's occupation number and frequency, then inspect its quantized energy ladder.

nodes.title: General Relativity and Cosmology
nodes.goal: Einstein's equations; the history of the universe.

quiz.prompt: Newton's theory has gravity act instantaneously across space, while general relativity makes changes in the field propagate at the speed of light. Suppose the Sun's mass could vanish at this instant. When would Earth's orbit begin to change?
quiz.answer: About eight minutes later, when the change reaches Earth.
quiz.explain: Gravitational influence travels at c, and the Sun is about 8.3 light-minutes away, so Earth would keep orbiting the absent Sun for that long. Removing Newton's instantaneous action is one of the things relativity does; gravitational waves, detected since 2015, arrive at the same speed as light.
choices: Instantly, since gravity is a property of mass, not a signal.
Never: Earth's orbit is held by its own inertia alone.
Gradually over many years, as spacetime slowly relaxes.
About eight minutes later, when the change reaches Earth.

quiz.prompt: In an expanding universe every observer sees distant galaxies receding, with recession speed proportional to distance. An astronomer on a galaxy 500 megaparsecs away turns their telescope on the Milky Way. What do they measure?
quiz.answer: Us receding from them at exactly the speed we measure for them.
quiz.explain: Hubble's law v = H d holds for every observer, so each sees the other receding at the same rate and neither sits at a centre. The expansion is space itself stretching, which is why it has no centre and no edge to be further from.
choices: Us receding from them at exactly the speed we measure for them.
Us at rest, since we sit at the centre of the expansion.
Us receding twice as fast, being further from the centre.
Us approaching, since expansion looks reversed from outside.

quiz.prompt: The cosmic microwave background is relic light released when the universe first became transparent, at about 3000 K — about the glow of a lamp filament. It arrives today peaking in the microwave band, at 2.7 K. What accounts for the change?
quiz.answer: Expansion has stretched its wavelength a thousandfold.
quiz.explain: Wavelengths stretch with the scale factor, so a 3000 K blackbody cools to 2.7 K while keeping its blackbody shape — a factor of about 1100, matching the redshift of last scattering. Dust would distort the spectrum, and the observed one is the most perfect blackbody ever measured.
choices: It has lost energy to dust along the way across the universe.
Expansion has stretched its wavelength a thousandfold.
It was always microwave: hot gas emits at long wavelengths.
Only the microwave part of the original glow still reaches us.

quiz.prompt: The Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c-squared is about 3.0 km for one solar mass. Give the Schwarzschild radius, in kilometres, of a black hole of 10 solar masses.
quiz.explain: The radius is directly proportional to mass, so ten solar masses gives 10 x 3.0 = 30 km.

quiz.prompt: Starlight grazing the Sun during an eclipse is deflected by 1.75 arcseconds, while treating light as a Newtonian projectile predicts only half that. State what the full result requires.
quiz.answer: Spacetime curvature, including the spatial part.
choices: Spacetime curvature, including the spatial part.
A larger value for the Sun's gravitational mass.
Refraction by the hot gas in the Sun's corona layer.
Assigning light a small but non-zero rest mass value.
quiz.explain: The Newtonian estimate captures only the time-time part of the metric. General relativity adds an equal contribution from curved space, doubling the deflection, as Eddington's 1919 measurement supported.

quiz.prompt: Cosmic inflation posits a brief burst of exponential expansion in the first fraction of a second. A rival proposal simply assumes the universe began uniform and flat, with no inflation. Which observation would tell the two apart?
quiz.answer: The particular spectrum of small density ripples in the CMB.
choices: Nothing: both give a uniform sky, so the two are equivalent.
The total age of the universe, which differs between them.
The particular spectrum of small density ripples in the CMB.
Inflation predicts a strongly curved universe, unlike the rival.
quiz.explain: Assuming uniformity explains nothing further. Inflation stretches quantum fluctuations to cosmic scale and so predicts a nearly scale-invariant, slightly tilted spectrum of density ripples with specific correlations — which has been measured and fits. Inflation drives curvature towards zero rather than creating it.

quiz.prompt: A galaxy recedes at 7000 km/s. Taking the Hubble constant as 70 km/s per megaparsec, what is its distance, in megaparsecs?
A spectral line emitted at 500 nm is observed at 600 nm. What is the redshift z?
A probe falling towards a black hole sends out regular pulses. A distant observer receives them ever further apart and sees the probe freeze at the horizon. What does the probe's own clock record?
quiz.answer: Crossing the horizon after a finite proper time.
choices: Freezing at the horizon, exactly as the distant view shows.
An infinite wait, because the horizon recedes ahead of it.
Crossing the horizon after a finite proper time.
A sudden halt as its clock is destroyed at the horizon.
quiz.explain: Horizon crossing takes finite proper time; the freezing is an artefact of the distant observer's coordinates and infinite gravitational redshift.

quiz.prompt: Type Ia supernovae at high redshift turn out fainter than a matter-only universe predicts. Which conclusion follows?
quiz.answer: The expansion of the universe has been accelerating recently.
choices: Those supernovae were intrinsically dimmer in the distant past.
Dust between the galaxies has absorbed much of their light.
The Hubble constant has been measured far too small.
The expansion of the universe has been accelerating recently.
quiz.explain: Extra faintness means extra distance for a given redshift. The dimming and dust alternatives were tested and disfavoured, leaving acceleration.

lesson_media.alt: A schematic coordinate grid curves near compact stress-energy beside expanding unbound galaxy separations and a stretched light wave.
lesson_media.caption: Stress-energy and geometry couple locally, while the cosmological scale factor expands unbound separations and redshifts wavelengths without a center.

lesson_media.title: Expanding Universe Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Change the observation epoch's scale factor to connect expansion with redshift.

nodes.title: Condensed Matter
nodes.goal: Superconductivity, phase transitions, emergence.

quiz.prompt: One sample is cooled below its critical temperature in zero field and a magnetic field is then switched on outside it. A second identical sample is cooled with the field already applied. What field does the Meissner effect predict inside each?
quiz.answer: Zero in both: flux is actively expelled, not merely kept out.
quiz.explain: A merely perfect conductor would freeze in whatever field was present when its resistance vanished, leaving the second sample with a trapped field. A superconductor instead drives flux out of its interior as it crosses Tc, so both end with zero inside. That is why the Meissner effect, not zero resistance, defines the state.
choices: Zero in the first, trapped in the second, as for a perfect conductor.
Zero in both: flux is actively expelled, not merely kept out.
Trapped in both: a superconductor cannot alter its inner field.
Zero in the second and trapped in the first, by Lenz's law.

quiz.prompt: Iron loses its magnetisation above 1043 K and water boils at 373 K. Both are phase transitions, but only one absorbs a latent heat at the transition temperature. Which one, and what does that tell you?
quiz.answer: Boiling: it is first order, taking in energy at fixed temperature.
quiz.explain: Boiling is first order: the density jumps and a latent heat goes in while the thermometer stands still. The Curie transition is continuous — the magnetisation falls smoothly to zero with no latent heat, though the heat capacity spikes. Latent heat is a thermodynamic quantity, not a chemical one.
choices: The magnetic loss: aligning spins costs energy at fixed temperature.
Boiling: it is first order, taking in energy at fixed temperature.
Both: every phase transition takes in a latent heat.
Neither: latent heat belongs to chemical change, not phase change.

quiz.prompt: A theorist can write down the exact equations for a single electron in a crystal, yet cannot obtain superconductivity from them. Condensed-matter physicists call superconductivity 'emergent'. What does that claim assert here?
quiz.answer: The ordering exists only in the collective behaviour of the many.
quiz.explain: Emergence means a property belongs to the many-body state and has no counterpart in one constituent, much as temperature belongs to a gas rather than to a molecule. Nothing new has to be added and the one-electron equations are not wrong; the collective solution simply is not visible in them.
choices: The single-electron equations must be wrong in some detail.
The ordering exists only in the collective behaviour of the many.
A further fundamental particle has to be added to the theory.
Superconductivity cannot be derived from physics at all.

quiz.prompt: Magnetic flux through a superconducting ring is quantised in units of h/2e = 2.07e-15 Wb. A ring is found to trap exactly 5 quanta. Give the trapped flux in units of 1e-15 Wb.
quiz.explain: 5 x 2.07 = 10.35, in units of 1e-15 Wb. The 2e in the denominator is direct evidence that the charge carriers are paired electrons.

quiz.prompt: A ceramic disc is cooled below its critical temperature with liquid nitrogen and a small magnet placed above it hovers in mid-air. Explain the levitation.
quiz.answer: Screening currents expel the field, repelling the magnet.
choices: Zero resistance on its own is enough to hold the magnet up.
Screening currents expel the field, repelling the magnet.
The sample turns into a permanent magnet as it is cooled.
The magnet is buoyed up by the cold dense air beneath it.
quiz.explain: A superconductor is more than a perfect conductor: it actively drives flux out of its interior, and the surface currents that do so create a field that repels the magnet above. Zero resistance alone would only hold whatever field was already there.

quiz.prompt: Iron heated past 1043 K loses its spontaneous magnetisation, and the loss becomes sharper the larger the sample. Characterise what happens at that temperature.
quiz.answer: A continuous transition; the ordering dies at T_c.
choices: A continuous transition; the ordering dies at T_c.
The iron melts into a non-magnetic liquid phase.
The atoms lose their individual magnetic moments.
The iron converts chemically into a new compound.
quiz.explain: Thermal agitation destroys the alignment between neighbouring moments while the moments themselves survive. The magnetisation falls continuously to zero, and true sharpness appears only in the large-system limit.

quiz.prompt: A superconductor has a critical temperature of 92 K, and liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. By how many kelvin does cooling with liquid nitrogen undercut the critical temperature?
quiz.explain: 92 - 77 = 15 K of margin.

quiz.prompt: A superconducting ring traps 3 flux quanta, each 2.07e-15 Wb. What total flux does it hold, in units of 1e-15 Wb?
quiz.explain: 3 x 2.07 = 6.21, in units of 1e-15 Wb.

quiz.prompt: A group reports a new material with zero resistance below 30 K, but it does not expel an applied magnetic field. As referee, what do you conclude?
quiz.answer: The claim is incomplete: a superconductor must also expel flux.
choices: Superconductivity is proved; flux expulsion follows automatically.
Zero resistance rules out any magnetic response, so the test was wrong.
The sample is simply a very pure metal at a low temperature.
The claim is incomplete: a superconductor must also expel flux.
quiz.explain: The Meissner effect is an independent signature, not a consequence of perfect conductivity, so both must be demonstrated.

quiz.prompt: Below its Curie point a ferromagnet must pick one direction for its magnetisation, although above it every direction has the same energy — spontaneous symmetry breaking. An amorphous ferromagnetic ribbon, which has no preferred crystal axis, is heated well past its Curie point and cooled again in zero field. What should you expect?
quiz.answer: A fresh direction, unrelated to the one it had before.
choices: The same direction, since the crystal axes fix the choice.
No magnetisation, since the symmetry has been restored.
A direction exactly opposite the one it started with.
A fresh direction, unrelated to the one it had before.
quiz.explain: The energy prefers no direction, so which one the sample takes is settled by whatever tiny fluctuation or stray field is present as it cools — a fresh accident each time. The magnetisation itself returns below Tc: it is the choice, not the ordering, that is arbitrary.

lesson_media.alt: History-dependent flux remains trapped in a perfect conductor while a type-I Meissner state below its critical field expels flux.
lesson_media.caption: Cooling below the critical temperature expels flux only within the critical-field regime; zero resistance alone does not define superconductivity.

lesson_media.title: Meissner Transition Lab
lesson_media.instructions: Vary temperature and applied field around a lead-like type-I phase boundary, then inspect whether the Meissner state persists.

nodes.title: Quantum Information
nodes.goal: Entanglement as a resource; qubits and algorithms.

quiz.prompt: Two qubits are prepared in a maximally entangled state. Alice measures her qubit and gets a definite result. What is true about Bob's qubit?
quiz.answer: Their outcomes are now correlated, but no message has been sent.
quiz.explain: Alice's outcome is random, so Bob's own statistics are unchanged and nothing is signalled. The correlation appears only when the two lists of results are compared over a classical channel, and it holds in a matched basis, not in every basis.
choices: Bob's qubit takes the same value as Alice's in any basis he picks.
Bob instantly receives a signal Alice chose, faster than light.
Their outcomes are now correlated, but no message has been sent.
Bob's qubit is entirely unaffected by Alice's measurement.

quiz.prompt: A start-up advertises a box that takes in a single qubit in an unknown state and emits two perfect copies of it. What is wrong with the offer?
quiz.answer: No device can copy an unknown quantum state.
quiz.explain: The no-cloning theorem follows from the linearity of quantum mechanics: a machine that copied two particular states correctly would fail on their superposition. Decoherence and entanglement supply are practical worries; this one is a matter of principle.
choices: It works, but the copies decohere within microseconds.
No device can copy an unknown quantum state.
Such a box needs entanglement it cannot supply on demand.
The copies are perfect, but the original is destroyed.

quiz.prompt: Three qubits are prepared in an equal superposition of all eight basis states. A student says the register therefore holds all eight numbers at once, so a single measurement will read them all out. Assess the claim.
quiz.answer: Wrong: a measurement returns one of the eight, chosen at random.
quiz.explain: The amplitudes really do describe all eight states, but measurement collapses the register to one three-bit string and repeating gives a fresh random one. Useful algorithms make the amplitudes interfere so the wanted answer becomes likely: the speed-up comes from interference, not from reading everything out at once.
choices: Right: that parallelism is where the quantum speed-up comes from.
Wrong: three qubits can only ever hold three of the eight states.
Wrong: a measurement returns one of the eight, chosen at random.
Right, provided the register is measured before it decoheres.

quiz.prompt: Describing the state of an n-qubit register takes 2 to the power n complex amplitudes. Give the number of complex amplitudes needed for 10 qubits.
quiz.explain: 2 to the tenth is 1024. The exponential growth is why classical simulation of a few dozen qubits already strains large computers.

quiz.prompt: Alice wants Bob to end up holding an unknown qubit state. She shares an entangled pair with him and performs a Bell measurement on her half plus the unknown qubit. State what Bob still needs.
quiz.answer: Two classical bits, sent no faster than light.
choices: Nothing at all: his qubit is already in the right state.
A second entangled pair, shared with Alice beforehand.
Two classical bits, sent no faster than light.
A copy of Alice's original qubit for comparison.
quiz.explain: Alice's Bell measurement has four possible outcomes, and Bob applies one of four corrections depending on which occurred. Needing that classical message is precisely why teleportation carries no signal faster than light.

quiz.prompt: A team runs Grover's algorithm on an unstructured database of a million entries and reports needing about a thousand queries, against roughly five hundred thousand for the best classical search. Assess the speed-up.
quiz.answer: Right: a quadratic speed-up is exactly what Grover gives.
choices: Right: a quadratic speed-up is exactly what Grover gives.
Wrong: Grover offers an exponential speed-up here.
Wrong: quantum search gives no advantage at all.
Right, but the advantage disappears for large sets.
quiz.explain: Grover needs about the square root of N queries, and the square root of a million is a thousand. The gain is real but only quadratic, unlike Shor's exponential advantage.

quiz.prompt: How many complex amplitudes are needed to describe the state of a 12-qubit register?
quiz.explain: 2 to the power 12 = 4096 amplitudes.

quiz.prompt: Grover's algorithm needs roughly the square root of N queries for an unstructured search of N items. Roughly how many queries for N = 1e8?
quiz.explain: The square root of 1e8 is 1e4, about 10000 queries.

quiz.prompt: A vendor claims their entangled pairs let two laboratories signal instantly across a continent. Diagnose the claim.
quiz.answer: Each side's outcomes look random alone, so no signal is carried.
choices: Each side's outcomes look random alone, so no signal is carried.
It works, but only while the pairs stay perfectly coherent.
It works at the speed of light rather than instantly.
The correlations do carry information once enough pairs are used.
quiz.explain: Local measurement statistics are unaffected by what the distant party does; correlations only appear once classical results are compared.

quiz.prompt: An engineer runs a nine-qubit algorithm on hardware with 0.5 percent error per two-qubit gate, and after a few hundred gates the output is indistinguishable from noise. What does this indicate?
quiz.answer: Errors accumulate faster than the computation can finish.
choices: Errors accumulate faster than the computation can finish.
The algorithm has been compiled with its gates out of order.
Nine qubits cannot represent enough states for the task.
The noise averages away if the circuit is run many times over.
quiz.explain: With a per-gate error of e, coherence survives roughly 1/e gates — about 200 here, which is the scale at which the output degrades. Beyond that a fault-tolerant encoding is needed; repetition alone does not undo coherent errors.

lesson_media.alt: Quantum teleportation routes two classical bits beside Bell-correlated measurements whose individual records remain random.
lesson_media.caption: Entanglement enables nonclassical joint statistics and state transfer, but neither produces faster-than-light signalling.

nodes.title: Open Problems
nodes.goal: Dark matter, quantum gravity, and what nobody knows yet.
articles: List of unsolved problems in physics

quiz.prompt: In a spiral galaxy nearly all the visible mass sits near the centre, so orbital speeds should fall off with radius the way the planets' do. Measured speeds instead stay roughly constant far out. What does that require?
quiz.answer: Unseen mass spread well beyond the visible disc.
quiz.explain: A flat rotation curve needs the mass enclosed within each radius to keep growing, so the extra mass has to lie out where the light does not. Piling it into the bulge would leave the outer curve falling. Each star orbits under the mass inside its own radius; none is dragged along by the others.
choices: Unseen mass packed into the galaxy's central bulge.
Unseen mass spread well beyond the visible disc.
A larger gravitational constant inside galaxies.
Nothing: the outer stars are dragged along by the inner ones.

quiz.prompt: General relativity treats spacetime as a smooth classical geometry, while quantum theory makes every dynamical field fluctuate. Where does that conflict first become unavoidable?
quiz.answer: Where curvature is extreme: black holes and the Big Bang.
quiz.explain: Both theories are superbly tested where they are normally applied, and they clash only where gravity is strong on a quantum scale. Quantum effects grow at high energy, not low, and everyday laboratories are exactly where both already work.
choices: In everyday laboratories, where both theories already fail.
At low energies, where quantum effects are at their strongest.
Nowhere: the two describe entirely unrelated phenomena.
Where curvature is extreme: black holes and the Big Bang.

quiz.prompt: A student proposes that more dark matter could account for the accelerating expansion, since dark matter and dark energy are both invisible. Why does that not work?
quiz.answer: Any mass attracts, so more of it would slow the expansion.
quiz.explain: Gravitational attraction from matter of any kind decelerates the expansion; acceleration needs something with negative pressure, which is what a cosmological constant supplies. Dark matter is abundant enough to shape galaxies and clusters, and like all matter it has both gravity and inertia.
choices: Dark matter is too thinly spread to affect expansion at all.
Any mass attracts, so more of it would slow the expansion.
Dark matter has gravity but no inertia, so it cannot push.
It does work; dark energy is just another name for it.

quiz.prompt: Ordinary matter makes up about 5 percent of the energy content of the universe and dark matter about 27 percent. Give the ratio of dark matter to ordinary matter, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 27 / 5 = 5.4. There is roughly five times as much dark matter as everything made of atoms.

quiz.prompt: In a pair of colliding galaxy clusters the X-ray-emitting hot gas, which holds most of the ordinary mass, has been left stranded between two clumps of mass mapped by gravitational lensing. What does that separation imply about the dominant mass?
quiz.answer: It is collisionless: it passed straight through the collision.
choices: It is the gas itself, and the lensing map carries an artefact.
It follows the visible matter, as modified gravity requires.
It is collisionless: it passed straight through the collision.
It was pushed aside by dark energy during the collision.
quiz.explain: Gas clouds ram into one another and slow, while collisionless matter flies on with the galaxies. The lensing mass staying with the galaxies rather than the gas separates most of the mass from most of the ordinary matter, which is what a collisionless dark component predicts and what gravity-modification models struggle to reproduce.

quiz.prompt: Some quantum-gravity models predict that photon speed depends slightly on photon energy. Observers time gamma-ray bursts billions of light years away and find high- and low-energy photons arriving together to within seconds. State what this rules out.
quiz.answer: Models with an energy-dependent light speed at the level probed.
choices: That gamma-ray bursts are genuinely distant.
That photons carry any energy whatsoever.
That general relativity holds at low energy.
Models with an energy-dependent light speed at the level probed.
quiz.explain: A billion-year flight would amplify a tiny speed difference into a large arrival gap. Seeing none constrains Lorentz-violating dispersion near and beyond the Planck scale.

quiz.prompt: Dark energy makes up about 68 percent of the universe's energy content and ordinary matter about 5 percent. How many times larger is the dark-energy share? Give one decimal place.
A galaxy's rotation curve stays flat out to large radius, for which the enclosed mass grows in proportion to radius. By what factor does the enclosed mass grow between 10 kpc and 30 kpc?
quiz.explain: Mass proportional to radius means the ratio is 30/10 = 3.

quiz.prompt: A direct-detection experiment runs for five years and records no dark-matter recoils. What has it established?
quiz.answer: Limits on the interaction cross-section, not absence.
choices: That dark matter does not exist after all.
That dark matter must be made of ordinary neutrinos.
That the galaxy's rotation curves were measured wrongly.
Limits on the interaction cross-section, not absence.
quiz.explain: A null result excludes a region of the mass and cross-section plane; it cannot rule out weaker couplings or different candidates.

quiz.prompt: A group proposes modifying gravity rather than adding dark matter. Which observation is hardest for such models to reproduce?
quiz.answer: Colliding clusters whose lensing mass sits away from the hot gas.
choices: The flat rotation curves of individual spiral galaxies.
Colliding clusters whose lensing mass sits away from the hot gas.
The observed brightness of distant supernovae.
The abundance of heavy elements in the oldest stars.
quiz.explain: Modified-gravity models are tuned to reproduce rotation curves, but a separation between the visible mass and the lensing mass points to a distinct, collisionless component.

lesson_media.caption: Dark-matter inference combines mismatched rotation speeds with lensing and collision evidence while retaining model uncertainty.
